papers.title: I-HITL: Inalienable Human-in-the-Loop
papers.abstract: Human oversight is a pillar of AI safety. It is often exercised by a human in the loop (HITL) who approves critical actions taken by an AI agent. AI agents' increasing ability to bypass guardrails, though, raises the question of how to enforce HITL robustly. We introduce the concept of inalienable human-in-the-loop (I-HITL). An I-HITL protocol ensures that an agent can initiate an action only with explicit human approval, even when the human interacts with a system (e.g., a local agentic harness) compromised by the agent. A strong I-HITL protocol additionally ensures such approval even when an adversarial human attempts to delegate approvals to an agent. To motivate I-HITL, we report on experiments with a popular agentic wallet platform in which raising an agent's spending cap requires HITL approval via emailed one-time passcodes (OTPs). Given access to the user's email and a task blocked by the cap, we find that ten different frontier models will often autonomously raise the cap, harvesting OTPs to bypass a HITL guardrail and surfacing other vulnerabilities. We formally define I-HITL using the concept of communication topologies and prove necessary and sufficient conditions for its realization. We show that an I-HITL protocol requires a trusted entity - a trusted computing device (or equivalent) - and characterize which such devices can and cannot realize an I-HITL protocol. We present a prototype I-HITL system called Countersign that can plug into and strengthen existing HITL systems using off-the-shelf consumer mobile devices.
papers.why: Proposes I-HITL protocol and Countersign system to enforce robust human oversight of AI agents by preventing guardrail bypass through formal guarantees and trusted devices.

idea.problem: AI agents can bypass human-in-the-loop approval mechanisms to execute unauthorized critical actions.
idea.approach: Define I-HITL protocol using communication topologies; prove necessary conditions; implement Countersign with trusted computing devices.
idea.result: Formal characterization of enforceable HITL; prototype system preventing agent approval delegation bypass.

papers.title: MarkovSim: an LLM Agent Harness with Bounded Context for Long-Horizon Computational Simulation
papers.abstract: Recent studies have applied large language model (LLM) agent systems to computational simulation workflows. Such workflows are long-horizon, so the information generated can exceed what an LLM can reason over at once, its context window. Context management is therefore essential, yet existing systems have either neglected it or treated it as a supporting mechanism rather than a subject of study. This paper presents MarkovSim, an LLM agent harness for long-horizon computational simulation, whose core is a context management scheme built into the workflow. The workflow record is written to a memory system with a predefined schema, and at workflow-defined boundaries, namely the state transitions of a finite-state machine a compact representation of the solution progress is constructed from it as the agent's context. Instantiated on finite element analysis and evaluated on six benchmark problems, MarkovSim passed 16 of 18 runs and corrected its own faults in both the solver operations and the model physics. The engineer was consulted only where engineering judgement was needed. The context remained bounded throughout every run, regardless of its length.
papers.why: Proposes an LLM agent harness with structured context management using finite-state machines and memory schemas to constrain information available to the agent during long-horizon computational tasks.

idea.problem: LLM agents cannot reason over context exceeding their window in long-horizon computational workflows
idea.approach: Build context management into agent harness using finite-state machine state transitions and memory schema to construct compact context…
idea.result: Passed 16/18 finite element analysis benchmark runs with bounded context throughout, self-correcting solver and physics errors

papers.title: RepoTrace: Improving Requirement Tracing in Multi-Round Agent Interactions
papers.abstract: Code agents have become increasingly capable of performing software engineering tasks through interaction with software environments. However, agents tend to degrade as the number of interaction rounds increases, making it difficult to maintain existing software during iterative modification. We analyze 2,656 agent trajectories in EvoCode-Bench and identify requirement focus misalignment as a recurring failure pattern, where agents struggle to distinguish the primary modification targets of a requirement from unrelated code. We propose Repotrace a requirement-driven repository understanding harness that combines repository structure with requirement semantics to construct a requirement-code correspondence and injects it into the agent context. This correspondence enables code agents to follow the repository architecture, trace requirements across multi-round interactions, and identify the core code elements corresponding to the current requirement. Experiments show that Repotrace improves the mean per-round reward (MPR) across different models (e.g., +19.99 on GLM-5.2) and agent harnesses (e.g., +10.22 on Claude Code). Across rounds, Repotrace increases the average per-round reward from 0.163 to 0.371 on Terminus-2 with DeepSeek-V4-Pro, while reducing average regression errors by 56.78%. We release the source code and agents' trajectories to support future research.
papers.why: Proposes a requirement-driven harness that injects requirement-code correspondence into agent context to constrain and guide code agent behavior across multi-round interactions.

idea.problem: Code agents degrade over multi-round interactions; fail to maintain requirement focus during iterative code modification
idea.approach: Build requirement-code correspondence by combining repository structure with requirement semantics; inject as context to guide agent
idea.result: Improves per-round reward across models and reduces regression errors by 56.78%

papers.title: CoSA: The Conflict of Skills Attack in Real-World LLM Agent Ecosystems
papers.abstract: Agent Skills allow LLM agents to combine reusable capabilities, but checking each Skill in isolation cannot rule out policy violations when they are composed. We term such failures Conflict of Skills (CoS): artifacts or assessment signals produced for one purpose may be reused downstream without preserving the restrictions or authorization needed for their new use. Using controlled executions of publicly available Skills and matched single-Skill controls, we identify four recurring mechanisms behind CoS. Building on these findings, we introduce the Conflict of Skills Attack (CoSA), which adds locally admitted Skills to an existing pool to supply missing business operations (capability supplementation) or reshape artifact exchange, decision reuse, and target/action bindings (relationship reshaping). CoSA leaves existing Skills and runtime permissions unchanged. To evaluate this threat under autonomous Skill selection, we introduce CoSA-Bench, built from real-world Skills and controlled services, with 288 tasks across recruiting, finance, IT, and business, covering data leakage, unauthorized state modification, and unsafe execution. Across five LLMs and three agent harnesses, additions capped at 5% of each original pool raise the policy-violation rate from 35.02% to 58.45%, an increase of 23.43 percentage points. Trace analysis links compliant-to-violating transitions to cross-Skill dependencies involving the additions. Finally, we develop a lightweight harness-level guard that checks information flow and authorization before consequential actions. On OpenClaw recruiting tasks across five models, the guard reduces violations from 65.28% to 6.67%, while policy-compliant task completion on matched benign controls changes from 66.67% to 65.00%.
papers.why: Identifies composition vulnerabilities in LLM agent skill pools and proposes harness-level guards that enforce authorization and information-flow constraints on agent actions.

idea.problem: Composing LLM agent skills can violate policies even when individual skills are safe due to cross-skill dependencies.
idea.approach: Design lightweight harness-level guard checking information flow and authorization before consequential actions; evaluate on real skills.
idea.result: Guard reduces policy violations from 65.28% to 6.67% on recruiting tasks while maintaining 65% benign task completion.

papers.title: AT-AT: Automatic Tool Optimization from Agent Traces
papers.abstract: Efforts to improve LLM-based agents typically focus on modifying the agent itself, yet success also depends on the environment in which an agent acts. Tools mediate this interaction: a tool's description shapes how an agent calls it, and its implementation determines the results and errors the agent receives afterwards. Many tools, such as APIs and MCP servers, are shared by many agents and maintained by providers who cannot change those agents. We introduce AT-AT (Automatic Tool Optimization from Agent Traces), an agentic tool optimizer that improves a shared toolset offline from historical agent executions while holding the agents fixed. A lightweight coding agent reads agent trajectories and their evaluation results, and selectively edits tool descriptions and, when permitted, implementations. On $τ^2$-bench-verified, AT-AT achieves the highest task completion rates in the Airline and Telecom domains at lower cost than strong prompt- and tool-optimizer baselines, and its Telecom gain is statistically significant under paired permutation tests. Optimizing the tools within a coding agent harness also improves held-out performance on TerminalBench-2 and TBLite. When applied to three production MCP servers at a large enterprise, AT-AT lowered cost or tool error rates on every server and increased held-out task passes on one. By turning accumulated execution traces into updates to shared tool environments, AT-AT provides a path toward continual improvement of agent systems through environment-side learning.
papers.why: Proposes a tool optimization harness that improves shared LLM-agent tools by editing descriptions and implementations based on agent traces, enabling better agent-environment interaction without modifying agents.

idea.problem: Shared tools (APIs, MCP servers) limit agent success but providers cannot modify agents using them
idea.approach: Automatic tool optimizer reads agent trajectories and selectively edits tool descriptions and implementations offline
idea.result: Improved task completion rates and reduced costs on benchmarks and production MCP servers

papers.title: SemaPLC: A Project-Grounded, Verification-Gated Agent Harness for PLC Code Generation
papers.abstract: In industrial practice, AI-generated programmable logic controller (PLC) code must integrate with existing projects and implement the required behavior across scan cycles. Compilation alone does not establish runtime behavior, and subsequent edits can invalidate earlier verification results. We present SemaPLC, a project-grounded, verification-gated agent harness for PLC code generation. The harness combines project context and reusable PLC skills with specification review, compilation, and live-runtime validation. Its completion gate requires recorded checks to meet acceptance criteria for the current implementation. Edits invalidate previous verdicts, and failed checks guide bounded repair. We evaluate SemaPLC on 117 independent-POU tasks and 65 project-context tasks across seven language-model backbones. SemaPLC outperforms the evaluated baselines on both metrics for every backbone. Its mean verified-pass rate and dynamic score reach 72.6% and 52.2, exceeding the strongest baseline means by 8.7% points and 20.8 points, respectively. Verification-layer and failure analyses reveal how build recovery and output observability affect end-to-end results and identify behavioral errors that remain after compilation. We apply the harness in KUKA's iiQworks product environment for PLC development and discuss engineering lessons for its industrial integration and deployment. The industrial use indicates the agent assistance substantially improves PLC development efficiency by 45%.
papers.why: Presents a verification-gated agent harness that constrains LLM-generated PLC code through specification review, compilation checks, and runtime validation gates, with structured repair feedback.

idea.problem: AI-generated PLC code must satisfy runtime behavior and project integration requirements; compilation alone cannot verify this
idea.approach: Agent harness combining project context, specification review, compilation, and live-runtime validation with completion gates and bounded repair
idea.result: 72.6% verified-pass rate and 52.2 dynamic score on 182 tasks; 45% efficiency improvement in industrial deployment

papers.title: EviACT: An Evidence-to-Action Framework for Agentic Program Repair
papers.abstract: LLM-based agents have moved automated program repair (APR) from fixed-context patch generation to interactive repository-level repair. However, existing agentic APR systems still struggle to use execution evidence to guide localization, patch generation, and validation. We propose EviACT (Evidence-to-Action), an agentic APR framework that coordinates three evidence-driven guardrails across repair stages. The retrieval scaffold grounds repair context, the compile gate filters invalid edits, and the test-driven gate checks target-test recovery before full regression. Across four benchmarks, EviACT improves resolve rate over the strongest reported comparable baselines by 1.6-6.0 percentage points and shows 70.1-88.6% lower reported per-bug API cost where baseline costs are available. Ablations and diagnostics suggest that these gains are associated with the coordinated evidence-to-action chain, making agentic APR more effective and efficient.
papers.why: Proposes evidence-driven guardrails (retrieval scaffold, compile gate, test-driven gate) that constrain and verify LLM-agent actions in automated program repair, enforcing checkable constraints on agent behavior.

idea.problem: LLM-based agents struggle to use execution evidence to guide localization, patch generation, and validation in program repair
idea.approach: Three coordinated evidence-driven guardrails: retrieval scaffold grounds context, compile gate filters invalid edits, test-driven gate validates patch…
idea.result: 1.6–6.0 pp improvement in resolve rate and 70–89% lower API cost versus baselines

papers.title: Learning Faithful Reasoning Processes with Spatio-Temporal Latent Dynamics for Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning has significantly enhanced the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs). However, existing reinforcement learning methods primarily optimize outcome-level rewards, providing limited supervision over the reasoning process. As a result, models may produce shortcut-prone or unstable reasoning trajectories even when the final answer is correct. We propose GeoFaith, a spatio-temporal latent dynamics framework for learning faithful reasoning processes without process reward models. GeoFaith combines final-state latent uncertainty, which measures whether a completed trajectory lies in a well-supported manifold region, with predictive-entropy dynamics, which penalize abnormal uncertainty patterns such as premature collapse, oscillation, and prolonged uncertainty. These signals are incorporated as process regularization into GRPO, jointly optimizing answer correctness and reasoning quality without step-level process annotations. Experiments show that GeoFaith consistently improves reasoning accuracy, produces more efficient reasoning trajectories, and outperforms both outcome-only reinforcement learning and process-supervision baselines.
papers.why: Proposes a framework to improve LLM reasoning fidelity by regularizing reasoning trajectories through latent dynamics, addressing shortcut-prone reasoning without explicit process supervision.

idea.problem: LLMs produce correct answers via unstable or shortcut-prone reasoning trajectories
idea.approach: Combine final-state latent uncertainty with predictive-entropy dynamics as process regularization in RL
idea.result: Improved reasoning accuracy, efficiency, and trajectory quality without process annotations

papers.title: Do Latent Tokens Think? A Causal and Adversarial Analysis of Chain-of-Continuous-Thought
papers.abstract: Latent tokens are gaining attention for enhancing reasoning in large language models (LLMs), yet their internal mechanisms remain unclear. This paper examines the problem from a reliability perspective, uncovering fundamental weaknesses: latent tokens function as uninterpretable placeholders rather than encoding faithful reasoning. While resistant to perturbation, they promote shortcut usage over genuine reasoning. We focus on Chain-of-Continuous-Thought (COCONUT), which claims better efficiency and stability than explicit Chain-of-Thought (CoT) while maintaining performance. We investigate this through two complementary approaches. First, steering experiments perturb specific token subsets, namely COCONUT and explicit CoT. Unlike CoT tokens, COCONUT tokens show minimal sensitivity to steering and lack reasoning-critical information. Second, shortcut experiments evaluate models under biased and out-of-distribution settings. Results on MMLU and HotpotQA demonstrate that COCONUT consistently exploits dataset artifacts, inflating benchmark performance without true reasoning. These findings reposition COCONUT as a pseudo-reasoning mechanism: it generates plausible traces that conceal shortcut dependence rather than faithfully representing reasoning processes.
papers.why: Analyzes internal mechanisms of latent tokens via steering and causal interventions to understand whether LLMs engage in genuine reasoning, revealing that latent tokens enable shortcuts rather than faithful reasoning.

idea.problem: Latent tokens claim to enhance reasoning in LLMs, but their internal mechanisms and reliability are unclear
idea.approach: Use steering experiments and shortcut detection to probe whether latent tokens encode faithful reasoning or exploit dataset artifacts
idea.result: Latent tokens function as uninterpretable placeholders that enable shortcuts rather than genuine reasoning

papers.title: Rethinking Verification in Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses enable large language models to act through tools, observe the results, and iteratively work toward a task goal. Verification checks and revises agents' work to improve output quality. Yet there is limited guidance on how harnesses should organize this effort. We study verification as an axis of test-time scaling by examining when to intervene, who checks the work, and how checking leads to revision. Our framework spans four layers of the agent lifecycle: initial instructions, mid-turn reminders, completion gates, and independent review. We compare 17 designs across seven frontier coding models on Terminal-Bench (TB) and SWE-bench Verified (SWE), and introduce VisualBench for expert evaluation of visual and interactive artifacts. Initial instructions and execution-time reminders yield modest, model-dependent average gains on the coding benchmarks, without substantially increasing average output token use. Completion gates can yield larger gains but may substantially increase cost. Independent review by a critic offers a more favorable accuracy-cost tradeoff, improving average accuracy by 5.9-9.5 percentage points on TB and 3.9-6.6 on SWE at 1.13-1.25 and 1.00-1.04 times baseline cost, respectively. On VisualBench, independent review achieves net preferences of 13.2-23.8 points over the baseline across its four designs, exceeding the evaluated L0-L2 designs. Additional review rounds or independent critics further improve average TB accuracy by up to 3.5 percentage points. Together, these results provide empirical guidance for verification design in agent harnesses and support independent review as a practical axis of test-time scaling.
papers.why: Systematically evaluates verification mechanisms for LLM agents across harness layers—instructions, reminders, gates, and independent review—to constrain and improve agent behavior at test time.

idea.problem: Limited guidance on how agent harnesses should organize verification to check and revise agent work
idea.approach: Empirically compare 17 verification designs across four lifecycle layers on coding benchmarks, measuring accuracy-cost tradeoffs
idea.result: Independent review achieves best accuracy-cost tradeoff, improving accuracy 5.9-9.5% on Terminal-Bench and 3.9-6.6% on SWE-bench at minimal cost…

papers.title: CTXAgent - Self-Controlled Context Management of LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses keep long sessions inside the context window by compacting the history when a token threshold is crossed. We study an alternative in which the model manages its own context: it decides when to compact, what to keep and what to write as the hand-off, given two tools and one paragraph of guidance. Since earlier work found that open-weight models cannot manage their own context without scaffolding, we compare seven frontier models under identical conditions, with and without the context tools, on token cost and benchmark score, and we compare our harness with three widely used harnesses on two of these models. The benchmark is assembled from existing ones: coding exercises, multi-step SciCode problems and SWE-bench Pro and Terminal-Bench 4.0 tasks are interleaved with planted facts, ephemeral observations and standing instructions, all checked deterministically, in sessions of 35-212 turns that resemble a user working through different tasks in one chat. Most of the strongest models manage their context: they compact and curate regularly, the live context of the mixed sessions stays mostly below 100k tokens, and their benchmark scores mostly do not drop significantly. For the models that manage their context well, the cost reduction is substantial but varies between models, because some models compact so often that other costs increase. With Claude Opus 5.5, the self-managed harness matches Claude Code on task success at 34% lower cost than its explicit 200k-window configuration and 49% lower than its default, with no context window to choose. We release the agent, the benchmark and all result rows.
papers.why: Studies how LLM agents can self-manage context windows using tools and guidance, comparing harness designs and evaluating token cost vs. performance across models and benchmarks.

idea.problem: Agent harnesses need to keep long sessions in context by compacting history when tokens exceed thresholds
idea.approach: Let models manage their own context via two tools and guidance, comparing seven frontier models with/without tools on cost and benchmark score
idea.result: Strongest models self-manage context effectively with substantial cost reduction (34-49% with Claude Opus) while maintaining benchmark performance

papers.title: SpeC2Rust: Specification-Driven Repository-Level C-to-Rust Translation
papers.abstract: Legacy C codebases remain central to system software and performance-critical infrastructure, but their weak memory safety imposes security and maintenance risks. Recent C-to-Rust translation systems, including LLM-based translators, make automated migration increasingly feasible, yet they still struggle to recover repository-level intent, avoid raw pointers and unsafe constructs, maintain cross-file interfaces, and repair compilation and validation failures efficiently. We propose SpeC2Rust, a specification-driven pipeline for repository-level C-to-Rust translation. It has three stages: (1) Project-Intent Structuring, which decomposes a C repository into semantically coherent modules and generates persistent repository- and module-level specifications; (2) Spec-Guided Generation, which translates each Rust module against these specifications with a live symbol registry to preserve cross-file consistency; and (3) Layered-Feedback Repair, which batches repairs and injects only failure-relevant diagnostics, specification context, and source evidence for efficient compilation and test-driven correction. We evaluate SpeC2Rust on eight repository-level C projects. It generates Rust projects that compile and pass the original end-to-end tests, with no raw-pointer declarations, raw-pointer dereferences, or unsafe lines. On projects shared with an LLM-based baseline, SpeC2Rust reduces cost by 66.1% and input-token usage by 84.7%.
papers.why: Extracts specifications from C repositories to guide Rust translation, using specification-driven code generation as an intermediate artifact for ensuring memory safety and cross-file consistency.

idea.problem: C-to-Rust translation struggles with repository-level intent, unsafe constructs, and cross-file consistency
idea.approach: Extract repository/module specifications, guide translation with specs and symbol registry, repair failures with spec-injected diagnostics
idea.result: Generated Rust projects compile with no unsafe code and pass original tests; 66% cost reduction vs LLM baseline

papers.title: Steering the Teacher: Improving On-Policy Self-Distillation for Thinking Models
papers.abstract: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) trains a student on its own reasoning trajectories using token-level supervision from a reference-conditioned teacher initialized from the same model. However, access to the reference can induce teacher behaviors that undermine independent reasoning in thinking models, leading to reference hallucinations, where the student cites an unavailable reference to justify reasoning steps, and reconsideration suppression, where the teacher discourages verification and revision at uncertain steps. We introduce Steered-Teacher OPSD (ST-OPSD) to jointly address these failure modes through activation steering. ST-OPSD extracts two directions from model-generated reasoning trajectories and applies them to the teacher's hidden states during distillation target computation, suppressing reference-invoking behavior and encouraging reconsideration with marker-family calibration. The student learns from the resulting teacher distributions without being steered. Experiments on AIME and HMMT show that ST-OPSD improves accuracy over vanilla OPSD and other interventions while restoring reconsideration and reference-hallucination rates to base-model levels.
papers.why: Uses activation steering to improve reasoning in language models by suppressing unwanted behaviors (reference hallucinations, reconsideration suppression) and encouraging sound independent reasoning during self-distillation training.

idea.problem: Self-distillation in thinking models causes reference hallucinations and suppresses verification/revision
idea.approach: Apply activation steering to teacher's hidden states during distillation, suppressing reference-invoking and encouraging reconsideration
idea.result: ST-OPSD improves accuracy on AIME/HMMT while restoring healthy reasoning behaviors

papers.title: EntailLLM: Verifying Agent-Generated Vulnerability Discovery Paths with Domain Knowledge via Logic Programming
papers.abstract: Large language model agents are increasingly used to analyze potential software vulnerabilities, but their outputs can silently violate domain knowledge, limiting their reliability in safety-critical settings such as medical devices. Prior work either treats that output as a prediction to be scored or constrains it to walks within a single knowledge graph; neither checks whether reasoning over a binary is entailed by an independent body of domain knowledge. We present EntailLLM, a framework that includes a specialized LLM agent and a validation mechanism. The agent proposes a traversal path of the function call graph for a vulnerability, which is checked against a separate knowledge graph and a logic program by an entailment procedure under annotated logic. We evaluate EntailLLM by examining six specialized agents across three CWE classes, and eight binaries varying in size from 405 to 12,696 functions. The agents improve pooled entailment from 77% to 98%, with entailment decreasing in only 3 of 118 configurations. We found that the best-performing agent combines self-refinement and a priori domain knowledge. EntailLLM is deployed end-to-end on real medical-device binaries, reaching 98% pooled entailment without per-device tuning. Our framework inherits the formal guarantees of generalized annotated logic, providing logical verification of agent output that is both explainable and grounded in well-defined semantics.
papers.why: Proposes a verification mechanism using logic programming to check whether LLM-agent outputs entail domain knowledge, grounding agent reasoning in formal semantics.

idea.problem: LLM agents analyzing vulnerabilities can silently violate domain knowledge, limiting reliability in safety-critical settings
idea.approach: Agent proposes function-call paths checked against knowledge graph and logic program via entailment under annotated logic
idea.result: Achieves 98% pooled entailment on real medical-device binaries with formal verification guarantees

papers.title: FlashScript: Compiling Recurring Agent Workflows into Reusable Neuro-Symbolic Programs
papers.abstract: Many agent tasks recur with new data or small changes, yet agents regenerate their reasoning and actions on each run, producing different results. Distilling a prior run into a skill helps the agent avoid earlier mistakes, but it still re-runs the full process each time, so runs can vary and incur that cost. We compile a successful agent run into a reusable neuro-symbolic program (NSP) with a set of guidelines we call FlashScript. Actions and data transformations become code, instance-specific values become parameters, and decisions that need model judgment become LLM calls. We identify three layers where these calls belong and three techniques that replace most of them with code. The compilation does not remove nondeterminism; it localizes it, so the deterministic program and its neural calls can be reviewed and tested separately. Across 120 WorkBench analytics tasks with Claude Haiku 4.5, the NSPs were correct and made identical tool calls on every run, using about 70 times fewer input tokens and a third of the runtime of a skill-guided agent whose runs were inconsistent. In a composite version of the tasks, the skill-guided agent's accuracy fell to 23%, and its output inconsistency increased, while the NSPs remained correct and identical across all runs. The NSPs successfully generalized to all 108 unseen instances of the same templates. Our findings suggest that NSPs from agent trajectories can be considered cumulative software assets for end-users to test, maintain, and reuse in their recurring workflows.
papers.why: Compiles agent runs into neuro-symbolic programs that localize nondeterminism and enable deterministic, reviewable, and testable agent behavior with structured guardrails around LLM calls.

idea.problem: Agent tasks regenerate reasoning and actions on each run, producing inconsistent results and token waste
idea.approach: Compile successful runs into neuro-symbolic programs with actions as code, values as parameters, decisions as localized LLM calls
idea.result: 70× fewer tokens, 1/3 runtime, consistent identical tool calls, successful generalization to unseen instances

papers.title: Numina Fuse: Interactive Autoformalization in Lean 4
papers.abstract: Numina Fuse is an agent-native application for formalizing mathematics in Lean 4. Since Lean can compile while not representing its intended informal meaning, and agents now write Lean faster than people can read it, we built Fuse around human supervision of agent work. A user works with an AI orchestrator on a Lean project and supervises it through views of the blueprint, the dependency graph, and the Lean code, while the backend keeps the project's derived state and runs agents for hours without the user present. We describe the development of Fuse throughout 2026, as it moved from a prescribed pipeline of agents paced by human review to an orchestrator that dispatches specialists, provers, and parallel children on its own. We designed for this shift, keeping project state, tooling, and interface design separate from orchestration so that agents could take over more of the work as models improved. We report Fuse's use in a formalization of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture and a study of prover models. We close with lessons for the next generation of autoformalization systems. Fuse Desktop, an open-source local version, is available at https://github.com/project-numina/fuse-desktop.
papers.why: Numina Fuse is an agent-native system for interactive autoformalization in Lean 4, designed around human supervision of LLM agents with structured oversight via blueprints, dependency graphs, and code views.

idea.problem: Lean agents write faster than humans can review, requiring supervision mechanisms to ensure correctness during autoformalization
idea.approach: Build an orchestrator with human-supervisory harness providing blueprint, dependency graph, and code views while managing agent dispatching and project…
idea.result: System used to formalize three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture; demonstrates scalable supervised autoformalization with shifting agent responsibilities

papers.title: Build or Adopt? Custom-Built vs. General-Purpose LLM Agent Harnesses for Automotive GUI Testing
papers.abstract: As general-purpose LLM agent harnesses mature, organizations must decide whether to continue developing in-house systems or adopt existing alternatives. We study this decision at Volvo Group for GUI testing of Android-based in-vehicle infotainment (IVI) systems. We compare a production, custom-built harness with two general-purpose harnesses, Claude Code and OpenCode, keeping the tools, accessed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), and the models the same. We evaluate the harnesses with up to four models on Volvo's IVI test cases and on open-ended tasks in public apps (Google Maps, Booking.com), and interview ten practitioners: developers, the product owner, and testers. On Volvo's stepwise IVI tests, general-purpose harnesses match the custom-built harness in success but vary more across runs. Their inference cost per task is 2.6-10.7 times higher, yet the engineering effort they save outweighs this: for a nightly IVI regression suite, total monthly cost, including engineering effort and inference, is 3-66% lower. On open-ended public-app tasks, they succeed more often, mainly because they recover better from incorrect actions. Interviews suggest that external advances can turn an in-house harness into technical debt even without deterioration. Adopting a general-purpose harness shifts maintenance from the agent loop to tools and instructions, but gives teams less control over what the model receives. Regardless of the harness, testers want to inspect the agent's actions and ensure that it follows the prescribed test scenario.
papers.why: Empirically compares custom-built vs. general-purpose LLM agent harnesses for GUI testing, analyzing their scaffolding, control mechanisms, tool interfaces, and practitioner needs for verification and inspection.

idea.problem: Organizations must choose between custom-built and general-purpose LLM agent harnesses for GUI testing tasks
idea.approach: Compare production custom harness with two general-purpose harnesses (Claude Code, OpenCode) on IVI tests and public-app tasks, including practitioner…
idea.result: General-purpose harnesses match custom harness on IVI tests but cost more in inference; save engineering effort; succeed more on open-ended tasks

papers.title: Navigating Epistemic Parity in LLM Agents: A Benchmark for Cross-Source Conflict Resolution Between Memory and Procedural Skills
papers.abstract: Production LLM agents increasingly run episodic memory pipelines and procedural skill modules (e.g., SKILL.md files) in tandem. Both are injected into the same context region with no defined precedence, so they can issue contradictory instructions that no instruction hierarchy resolves, a condition we term epistemic parity. We introduce a benchmark for measuring how LLM agents adjudicate such cross-source conflicts. We (i) develop a four-way taxonomy of memory-skill contradictions (factual, format, procedural, permission); (ii) instantiate 52 scenarios under a tripartite test-case anatomy (memory injection, skill injection, ambiguous user task), scored almost entirely by deterministic checkers over tool-call payloads and output structure; and (iii) run each scenario under three context conditions to isolate positional bias, measure the efficacy of an explicit precedence directive, and classify disclosure behavior, quantifying silent adjudication: resolving a conflict without telling the user. Across 1,383 runs on three open-weight models, neither source wins uniformly: resolution depends jointly on conflict type, model, and injection order. Moving the skill block nearer the task raises its win rate in all six factual and procedural cells (sign test, p = 0.031) but reverses for format conflicts, indicating that adjudication tracks token placement rather than source semantics. An explicit "skill takes absolute precedence" directive raises skill compliance on the two stronger models yet leaves 3-10% residual non-compliance, and moves the smallest model's factual and procedural resolution in the wrong direction. Most consequentially, in 98.8% of runs where the agent acted through a tool call it emitted no accompanying text at all, and 89% of all runs disclosed nothing about the contradiction: silent adjudication is the default. Code, scenarios, and raw outputs are public.
papers.why: Systematically evaluates how LLM agents resolve conflicts between contradictory instructions from memory and procedural skills, a guardrailing challenge; proposes a taxonomy and benchmark for measuring agent behavior under conflicting constraints.

idea.problem: LLM agents receive contradictory instructions from episodic memory and procedural skills with no defined precedence hierarchy
idea.approach: Create taxonomy of four conflict types and benchmark measuring agent adjudication across context conditions and models with deterministic scoring
idea.result: Resolution depends on conflict type, model, and injection order; explicit precedence directives partially effective; agents silently adjudicate in 89% of…

papers.title: SemantEq: Faithful Bidirectional Equivalence of Formal Statements
papers.abstract: Statement autoformalization translates mathematics from natural language into a proof assistant such as Lean 4, and models now do it at scale. As provers get stronger, the burden of correctness shifts from the proof to the statement, that is, to whether the formal statement faithfully translates its source. Given a trusted reference formalization, the natural test is logical equivalence, and it proves too much. $P \leftrightarrow Q$ holds trivially for any two statements $P$ and $Q$ that the library proves, because a prover can prove each separately and pass through $P \leftrightarrow \mathrm{True} \leftrightarrow Q$. The stronger the prover, the more unrelated pairs pass. Earlier methods restrict the prover and check that each proof names the other statement. We introduce SemantEq, a more principled relation that instead requires each statement to turn into the other only through a chain of allowed steps, such as logical rearrangement and rewriting with the library's own equations. Our programs judge a proof by the proof term Lean checks, not by its tactic script. SemantEq-Eval, a search without a model, reaches 100% precision and 65.6% recall on the ProofNetVerif test split under our adjudicated labels, against 95.8% and 61.8% for BEq+, and an 8.9-fold increase in its CPU time adds at most three pairs. A language model finds more proofs, but under two of four prompts it proves both directions of about two in five of the non-equivalent pairs. SemantEq-ProofAudit audits each model-written proof under a policy derived from the relation and accepts none of the 104 non-equivalent pairs, and it raises recall on 407 equivalent pairs from 65.4% to 81.1% under the best prompt. Separating the generation of equivalence proofs from their acceptance lets a stronger prover raise recall without changing what an acceptance means. We release code and data at: https://github.com/hlxr89/SemantEq
papers.why: Proposes SemantEq, a principled method to verify that formal statements faithfully translate natural-language source via logical equivalence checking with proof-term auditing.

idea.problem: Autoformalized statements may not faithfully translate natural-language source; logical equivalence is too weak a test.
idea.approach: Require equivalence proofs to use only allowed steps (logical rearrangement, library rewrites); audit proof terms under derived policy.
idea.result: 100% precision, 65.6% recall; proof auditing achieves 81.1% recall on equivalent pairs while rejecting all non-equivalent pairs.

papers.title: HarnessMM: Recursive Self-Improvement for Harness Token Efficiency
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses repeatedly invoke reasoning after tool feedback, even when an earlier call has already fixed the next action. We introduce HarnessMM (Harness Minus Minus), a method for improving harness token efficiency through guarded decision reuse and recursive self-improvement (RSI). RSI iteratively refines companion harness configurations from training feedback, with validation selecting the configuration for deployment. A controller at the model-tool boundary reuses resolved decisions to replace later reasoning callbacks while actor weights remain fixed. Executable Decision Graphs store exact actions, literal arguments, causal dependencies, and public guards. Guarded Decision Reuse activates these persistent decisions from observed receipts; Certified Callback Substitution executes them through the native interface and records removal of the registered slow callback. New semantic decisions, unsupported evidence, and selector abstention invoke the original actor again. The representation restricts what feedback may change, while complete-task measurements establish quality and cost. On HumanEval, HarnessMM preserves Codex success at 90.82\% while reducing Tokens/task (k) from 66.72 to 47.02 (29.54\% saving). For DeepSeek Harness, success rises from 71.43\% to 85.71\% while Tokens/task (k) fall from 96.28 to 11.62 (87.93\% saving). A separate MBPP ablation measures 26.91\% lower cost than single-use graphs and 19.52\% lower cost than retained callbacks. These results establish guarded decision reuse as a practical way to reduce repeated reasoning in existing harnesses.
papers.why: Proposes a harness-level control mechanism (HarnessMM) that reuses and guards decisions at the model-tool boundary to reduce redundant reasoning callbacks while maintaining task correctness.

idea.problem: Agent harnesses repeatedly invoke reasoning after tool feedback even when earlier decisions resolve the next action
idea.approach: Guarded Decision Reuse via Executable Decision Graphs with guards, plus Recursive Self-Improvement for harness configuration
idea.result: 29.54% token savings on HumanEval, 87.93% on DeepSeek while preserving or improving success rates

papers.title: LGMT: A Tool for Testing the Logical Reasoning Reliability of LLMs
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) increasingly serve as reasoning components in modern software systems, yet a model that answers a logical query correctly can contradict itself when the same problem is restated in an equivalent form. Static benchmarks evaluate queries in isolation and therefore fail to expose such inconsistencies. To address this limitation, we present LGMT, an open-source tool that detects reasoning inconsistencies through metamorphic relations grounded in first-order logic. Given a source test case in premise-conclusion form, LGMT generates logically equivalent follow-up cases and checks whether the model's entailment predictions agree across the pair, without ground-truth labels. The tool provides 20 built-in metamorphic relations, supports custom ones verified by the Z3 theorem prover, and runs from a CLI or a web studio, including an offline mock mode requiring no API key. Across six widely used LLMs on a bundled benchmark of 3,091 metamorphic groups, LGMT reveals inconsistency rates ranging from 20.84% to 29.44%. LGMT is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/MaxwelsDonc/lgmt-tool, with a demonstration video at https://youtu.be/gou4opptu1U.
papers.why: Develops a testing tool to detect logical reasoning inconsistencies in LLMs using metamorphic relations grounded in first-order logic, directly addressing semantic reasoning reliability.

idea.problem: LLMs contradict themselves on logically equivalent reasoning problems despite correct answers on isolated queries
idea.approach: Generate logically equivalent test cases via metamorphic relations verified by Z3 theorem prover; check consistency of entailment predictions
idea.result: Reveals 20.84-29.44% inconsistency rates across six LLMs; tool released with 20 built-in relations and custom relation support

papers.title: Trial by Trace: Benchmarking AI Agent Harnesses for Reliability and Failure Attribution
papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used to solve real-world problems, and their effectiveness depends on both the underlying models and the harnesses that support their operation. However, most existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities and overall agent performance, with limited attention to the evaluation of agent harnesses. To address this gap, we introduce TraceTrial-Bench, which organizes harness reliability into seven components covering context, execution, governance, lifecycle, observability, tools, and verification. We construct 95 expert-level, mechanism-oriented tasks with executable or state-based ground truth to support semantically equivalent comparisons while preserving the native behavior of each harness. We design a Trajectory Tracing (TT) module to capture agent execution traces and introduce a two-layer evaluation framework that separately assesses agent performance and harness reliability. In addition, we design a Multi-source Evidence Acquisition (MEA) module to provide evidence from the agent context, harness, and execution environment for LLM-based evaluation, and develop a Failure Attribution (FA) module that uses explicit mechanism chains to support attribution at the run level. Across 4 harnesses, 9 models, and 95 tasks, our evaluation of 3,420 runs yields macro-averaged harness scores ranging from 59.8% to 72.0%, while 31.1% of runs achieve task success despite failing at least one harness criterion. TraceTrial-Bench provides an auditable and reproducible foundation for comparing agent harnesses, diagnosing their failures, and studying how harness design interacts with model behavior.
papers.why: Introduces a benchmark for evaluating LLM agent harnesses on reliability components including governance, verification, and observability, with failure attribution mechanisms to assess agent constraints and controls.

idea.problem: Existing benchmarks focus on model capabilities, not harness reliability and failure attribution in LLM agents
idea.approach: TraceTrial-Bench organizes harness reliability into seven components with trajectory tracing, multi-source evidence acquisition, and failure attribution…
idea.result: Evaluation across 4 harnesses and 95 tasks shows harness scores 59.8-72.0%, with 31.1% of runs succeeding despite harness criterion failures

papers.title: Pairing Matters: Performance, Failures, and Efficiency in Lightweight Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Self-hosting coding agents is often necessary for software-engineering teams that must keep proprietary code and development traces within controlled infrastructure. Lightweight, open-weight models make such deployment more feasible by reducing hardware requirements, while strong results on repository-level benchmarks demonstrate their potential for demanding coding tasks. Deploying these models as coding agents requires pairing them with an agent harness, making their joint performance a key deployment consideration. Yet existing leaderboards primarily report fixed harness-model configurations rather than controlled comparisons across alternative pairings. To address this gap, we investigate harness-model interactions through a controlled full-factorial evaluation of six open-source harnesses and three lightweight coding models across 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, producing 1,800 graded runs under common serving, metering, and grading conditions. For the same model, resolution rates differ by up to 44 percentage points across harnesses, while harness rankings change across models. We apply an evidence-based failure taxonomy to 1,100 unsuccessful runs and find substantial differences in failure patterns across harness-model pairings. A model's dominant failure modes under one harness need not dominate under another. Efficiency is similarly dependent on the pairing: even among model-directed loop harnesses, charged tokens per resolved task vary by more than 20-fold. These findings make harness-model selection a central deployment decision for lightweight coding agents. Strong performance with one harness or model does not guarantee similar results with another. We translate these findings into practitioner guidance for pairing selection, token-efficiency assessment, and trajectory-informed harness engineering, and release the complete experimental records and analysis artifacts.
papers.why: Systematically evaluates how agent harnesses interact with and constrain lightweight coding models, providing evidence-based guidance on harness-model pairings for practical agent deployment.

idea.problem: Agent harness-model pairings have up to 44pp performance variance, but existing leaderboards don't evaluate their interactions
idea.approach: Full-factorial evaluation of 6 harnesses × 3 models across 100 SWE-bench tasks with taxonomy of failure modes
idea.result: Harness-model pairing is critical; token efficiency and failure patterns vary 20-fold; released experimental records and guidance

papers.title: Are LLM-Generated Formal Specifications Faithful to Their Requirements? A Study on Bimodal Formal Specification Generation
papers.abstract: Formal specification generation is a critical step towards formal verification and correctness assurance of software. Recently, large language models have been widely adopted in automatic generation of formal specifications. However, existing LLM-based specification generation approaches often assume that the input program is correct, which deviates from the real purpose of formal verification---to figure out whether the program meets its requirements when its correctness is unknown. Therefore, we conduct an empirical study of LLM-based specification generation under the bimodal setting: given both the natural language requirement and its corresponding code implementation, whose correctness is unknown. We construct a benchmark of 1,403 C programs and evaluate ACSL specification generation with Frama-C verification. Our study reaches several interesting findings: first, when the code implementation is correct, providing the natural language requirement does not further improve the pass rate of generated specifications. Second, when the code implementation is incorrect, LLM-based specification generation may erroneously pass verification by producing weak or implementation-misled specifications, and this cannot be fully alleviated by advanced prompting approaches. Compared with the non-formal HoarePrompt approach, LLM-generated formal specifications are less effective in predicting requirement-code consistency. Our study takes a first look at applying LLM-based formal specification generation to verifying program correctness against requirements, and points to requirement-faithful specification generation as a new direction for future LLM-based formal specification research.
papers.why: Empirically evaluates LLM-based formal specification generation (ACSL) for faithfulness to natural-language requirements, identifying failure modes in detecting requirement-code inconsistencies.

idea.problem: LLM-generated formal specs may not faithfully reflect requirements, especially when code is incorrect
idea.approach: Benchmark ACSL spec generation on C programs with known correctness, evaluate with Frama-C verification
idea.result: LLMs generate weak specs that pass verification despite requirement-code mismatch; requirements poorly improve specs for correct code

papers.title: Do AI-for-Science Agents Preserve Model Safety?
papers.abstract: AI-for-Science agents are increasingly being used for formulating scientific hypotheses, running autonomous experiments, and interpreting evidence. These agents are constructed by integrating a large language model (LLM) into a domain-specific agent harness, which in turn can improve the LLM's scientific capability and enable the model to orchestrate scientific tools. In this work, we ask whether model safety is preserved when an LLM is integrated in an AI-for-Science agent harness. We evaluate five agent harnesses on 50 harmful chemistry requests. Specifically, we study how the safety behavior changes under direct prompting, two simple adversarial prompting strategies, and an adaptive attack. Across four recent GPT variants, our results show that the agent harness can increase harmful compliance even under direct prompting. More critically, we find that adaptive attacks that are largely unsuccessful against the base LLM suddenly become highly successful after the agent harness is introduced. Our results show that the safety behavior of the base LLM is not durable once a harness is introduced. Thus, as AI-for-Science agents become more capable and autonomous, the community needs to evaluate and align the agent using domain-specific safety benchmarks.
papers.why: Evaluates how agent harnesses affect LLM safety and adversarial robustness, identifying guardrail gaps when models are integrated into agent scaffolding.

idea.problem: LLM safety guarantees may not hold when models are integrated into agent harnesses
idea.approach: Evaluate five agent harnesses on harmful chemistry requests using direct and adaptive attacks
idea.result: Agent harnesses increase harmful compliance; adaptive attacks succeed after harness integration but fail on base models

papers.title: VeriFin: A Neurosymbolic Framework for Verifying LLM-Generated Financial Claims
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are being adopted in financial workflows, where accuracy and reliability are critical. One such application is financial question answering over public company filings. However, LLMs struggle with quantitative financial reasoning, including identifying financial facts, interpreting reporting periods and units, and determining appropriate metrics, leading to incorrect answers. Recent RAG-based methods have improved financial question answering but do not ensure factual and numerical correctness. LLM-based verifiers may also accept incorrect numerical claims. To address this, we introduce VeriFin, a neurosymbolic framework for verifying LLM generated numerical financial claims. Given a question and a generated answer, VeriFin retrieves filing evidence, grounds values in XBRL facts, and establishes the required formula independently of the answer. It then uses the Z3 SMT solver to check the resulting arithmetic constraints. VeriFin accepts consistent claims, rejects inconsistent claims, and abstains when required facts or formulas cannot be established. To evaluate VeriFin, we constructed XBRLFiling, a dataset of 600 numerical questions from corporate filings, and selected 67 and 403 questions from FinanceBench and TAT-DQA, respectively. Across six answer models and three datasets, VeriFin achieves 100% observed precision among accepted answers with known correctness. For Qwen3-30B on XBRLFiling, VeriFin accepts 304 correct answers compared to 166 for an LLM judge, while reducing false accepts from 87 to 0. We release our benchmark to support research on reliable financial question answering.
papers.why: Proposes a neurosymbolic framework using SMT solvers to verify numerical financial claims by formalizing arithmetic constraints, grounding LLM outputs in structured data, and checking consistency—combining formal verification with LLM reasoning.

idea.problem: LLMs generate incorrect financial answers due to poor quantitative reasoning and fact grounding
idea.approach: Extract and formalize numerical claims into SMT constraints, ground values in XBRL facts, verify with Z3 solver
idea.result: Achieves 100% precision on accepted answers; reduces false accepts from 87 to 0 on benchmark dataset

papers.title: Injection-Execution Dissociation: A Mechanistic Evaluation of Persistent Memory Attacks and Defenses in Stateful LLM Agents
papers.abstract: In LLM agents with persistent memory, whether a model stores an injected instruction and whether it later acts on it are separable safety properties. We call this the injection-execution dissociation. We evaluate 29 frontier endpoints with the malicious document in the retrieval corpus (N=10 each, four topped up to N=40; an earlier bug-affected collection is superseded). Execution is common: 7 endpoints exfiltrate in at least 9 of 10 runs and 11 more in some but fewer. Zero exfiltration is weak evidence of resistance: GPT-5.4, GPT-5.6-sol and Claude Haiku 4.5 never exfiltrate in 40 draft-only runs each but send almost no email, and in an exploratory follow-up that supplies the content and asks for a send they exfiltrate in 20 of 20, 5 of 20 and 6 of 20 runs. Anthropic's Opus and Sonnet models mostly store no forwarding directive and exfiltrate in at most 1 of 10 draft-only runs. We test six defences at four architectural layers in a 5,040-run factorial on nine open-weight models (N=40 per cell); these models store the instruction in every run, so it tests execution only. Input filters never see the payload, which arrives through retrieval. Retrieval-layer classifiers see it but, at the small operating points tested, do not flag it; frontier judges did. Only Memory Sandbox, which removes the recall tool, blocks the attack (0% ASR for eight of nine models). It is bypassed when a model rebuilds the instruction from the retrieval corpus: three Bedrock-served models do so (32.5-97.5% ASR), and a causal-mediation study on two OpenAI models attributes every success under the sandbox to this path. Stored but dormant instructions may create a cross-model risk; transfer was not demonstrated. Defences should be evaluated at both stages.
papers.why: Evaluates defense mechanisms against persistent-memory attacks on LLM agents across architectural layers, demonstrating which guardrails succeed or fail and identifying attack bypass techniques.

idea.problem: LLM agents with persistent memory are vulnerable to injected malicious instructions that can be stored and executed later
idea.approach: Systematically test injection-execution dissociation across frontier and open-weight models; evaluate six defenses at four architectural layers; use causal-mediation analysis to…
idea.result: Only Memory Sandbox fully blocks attacks on open-weight models; frontier models show variable resistance; models can rebuild instructions from retrieval corpus to bypass…

papers.title: PaperFormalizer: Author-in-the-Loop Autoformalization of Research Papers in Lean
papers.abstract: Even a carefully proofread paper can leave small gaps in its proofs or its stated assumptions. We introduce PaperFormalizer, a Lean-based agentic pipeline that helps authors find and close such gaps in their own papers and turn each paper into a Lean-verified version. Starting from the LaTeX source, PaperFormalizer transcribes the paper into a dependency graph of statements, audits each statement in natural language for faithfulness, ambiguity and correctness, and then formalizes and proves the statements in Lean against Mathlib, optional domain libraries and the author's personal toolkit. Only the author knows what a statement is meant to say and how a formalization gap in a result is best fixed. The pipeline therefore stops and asks the author whenever a statement admits more than one reading, presents every repair, in natural language and TeX symbols, as a proposal that the author can accept, decline or redirect, and leaves to the author every decision that could potentially change what the paper claims. The output is an annotated and revised version of the paper, a report of the changes, and Lean code in which each declaration is linked to the statement it formalizes. The author's toolkit grows as more papers are formalized, and authors can share their verified papers so that researchers who build on them can reuse their Lean code. By making verified papers practical to produce, PaperFormalizer aims to make research that rests on mathematical proofs more robust. PaperFormalizer runs inside a coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) and is available at https://github.com/Jiyuan-Tan/PaperFormalizer. Papers with Lean code shared by users are available at https://paperformalizer.org.
papers.why: Automates translation of mathematical proofs from LaTeX papers into Lean code, with author-in-the-loop verification and gap detection.

idea.problem: Mathematical papers contain proof gaps and ambiguous statements despite careful review
idea.approach: Agent pipeline that transcribes LaTeX to statements, audits for faithfulness, formalizes in Lean with author review at ambiguities
idea.result: Verified Lean code linked to paper statements; reusable toolkit for authors building on formalized work

papers.title: Certified Execution Harness for Agentic AI: Safe and Least-Intrusive Petri-Net Supervisory Control Between Reasoning and Action
papers.abstract: This paper studies the problem of safe tool execution for large language model (LLM) agents under prompt injection. Using Petri nets, we formalize the execution harness between the LLM and its tools as a supervisory control problem, in which marks represent capabilities, approvals and budgets. Since a transition fires only if the marks it needs are present, an injected request whose preconditions are unmet or already spent is refused regardless of its wording. Treating tool outcomes as uncontrollable, we enforce safety by the conventional maximally permissive supervisor, and this safety transfers to the running system under four assumptions. Moreover, to capture an agent that may propose again after a refusal, we introduce the notion of a replanning closed loop, in which each retry costs an inference call. We show that, in this loop, the conventional supervisor can be arbitrarily more intrusive than a stricter safe one. Furthermore, for a given proposer model, the maximally permissive least-intrusive supervisor is characterized as a value-threshold refinement of the conventional one. Under precise conditions, this refinement orders two concurrent actions by at most one monitor place. On an autonomous release agent, we find by synthesis that safe deployment requires a step that the supervisor can refuse after a rollout starts.
papers.why: Formalizes LLM agent execution as Petri-net supervisory control to enforce safety guardrails against prompt injection and budget violations through external architectural constraints.

idea.problem: LLM agents vulnerable to prompt injection and uncontrolled tool execution
idea.approach: Formalize execution harness using Petri nets with supervisory control enforcing resource marks and preconditions
idea.result: Safe supervisor design that minimizes refusals while preventing unsafe execution regardless of prompting

papers.title: SCOPE: Compiling Natural-Language Policies into Neurosymbolic Predicate Programs
papers.abstract: Policy enforcement for LLM agents has shifted from single-turn content moderation to compound, application-specific policies evaluated over multi-turn transcripts and tool-call trajectories. Fine-tuned guardrail models are efficient but degrade on compound policies, and while LLM-as-a-judge approaches achieve higher accuracy, they incur high inference cost and tend to produce unstable predictions. Neurosymbolic methods offer a natural alternative, decomposing the policy into narrow neural decisions composed under explicit logic. However, existing symbolic layers lack the required expressiveness and are optimized against fixed data rather than the policy itself. To address this, we introduce SCOPE, which compiles a policy into an executable program of neural predicates executed by small models, deterministic extractors, and code that composes their outputs. The program is optimized jointly with its training data, using adversarial generation of counterexamples that target where the program deviates from the policy. We evaluate SCOPE on a benchmark of real-world policy tasks against prompt optimization, task decomposition, and workflow generation methods, achieving the highest average accuracy across tasks and models. Programs optimized with the weakest executor transfer to other models without further optimization. This allows them to be deployed in production on inexpensive models, where they reach accuracy comparable to frontier reasoning models. Unlike these monolithic models, SCOPE produces substantially more stable predictions, and each verdict is interpretable through the predicate outputs that produced it. Additionally, we validate the key components of our method through an ablation study. SCOPE thus enables reliable, interpretable, and efficient policy enforcement at production scale.
papers.why: Compiles natural-language policies into executable neurosymbolic programs for interpretable, verifiable agent policy enforcement with neural and symbolic composition.

idea.problem: LLM-based policy enforcers are unstable, expensive, or inaccurate on compound multi-turn policies
idea.approach: Compile policies into executable programs of neural predicates and logic, optimized with adversarial counterexamples
idea.result: Higher accuracy than LLM-as-judge, stable predictions, interpretable verdicts, efficient deployment on small models

papers.title: UniGuard: Multi-View Guardrail Learning for Cross-Interface Safety Generalization
papers.abstract: Guardrail models are increasingly used as safety layers for LLMs and agentic systems, but most are trained on fixed prompt or response interfaces and become unreliable when the same safety case appears as a conversation, agent trajectory, multi-agent trace, or policy-conditioned input. We propose UniGuard, a training framework that learns interface-invariant safety representations from multiple semantically aligned views of the same safety case. We also construct the UniGuard-FT dataset by transforming 1,000 public safety cases into prompt, response, multi-turn conversation, agent-trace, and multi-agent-trace views, and train UniGuard-0.6B with classification, supervised contrastive learning, and asymmetric confidence calibration losses. Across unseen-interface benchmarks ATBench, PolicyGuardBench, and DynaBench, UniGuard-0.6B improves over its pretrained guardrail by 45.12 F1 points on average and reduces expected calibration error by 35.41 points, while remaining competitive with much larger guardrails such as Claude-Sonnet-4.5 and GPT-5.2 - despite being a 0.6B model and trained only with synthetic data.
papers.why: Proposes UniGuard, a training framework for guardrail models that enforce safety constraints across diverse agent interfaces and input representations, enabling robust safety verification for agentic systems.

idea.problem: Guardrail models fail when safety cases appear in different interface formats (conversations, agent trajectories, policies)
idea.approach: Train interface-invariant representations using multiple semantically aligned views and contrastive learning losses
idea.result: UniGuard-0.6B improves F1 by 45.12 points on average across unseen-interface benchmarks, competitive with larger models

papers.title: From Clinical Judgment to Checkable Rules: Clinician-Led Guardrails for Mental-Health Chatbots
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in mental-health contexts can be evaluated for safety failures, but the resulting judgments are often difficult to inspect or explain. Common approaches to improving safety rely on prompt engineering, LLM-as-a-Judge, and Constitutional AI. In this work, we describe a clinician-led alternative in which two clinicians define, finalize, and adjudicate the four safety checks of a rule base, which is formally verified for internal consistency and applied as a guardrail over LLM outputs. Here and in the title, clinician-led refers to this rule base, not to the fact extractor or the uncertainty default, which are ours. Every verdict of the resulting verification layer is recomputable from a named rule and sixteen facts. Against an LLM judge matched in model, revision, quantization, rule text, and decoding but without the layer's computed 988/911 fact, the largest disagreement class, the satisfied-rule class, is structured: the Llama-3.3-70B judge, on its primary prompt, demands a crisis resource from 55 of the 65 replies (84.6%) that already contain one, while the same model, asked as a fact extractor, reports a recognized resource present on 54 of the 55. The verification layer never raises that demand, by construction. We report with equal prominence where this judge is stronger: fewer false crisis alarms on the one reference-scored check. We also report the measured cost (a specification revision raised block-class outcomes on held-out boundary prompts of an over-refusal benchmark from 6.0% to 16.0%, chiefly by changing fact extraction), the clinicians' decision to keep our uncertainty default, and the analysis of the result. The contribution is not a safer verdict. It is a guardrail whose disagreements with the judge localize to named rules and facts and whose measured costs trace to named facts and the uncertainty default.
papers.why: Proposes a clinician-led rule base applied as a formally verified guardrail over LLM outputs for mental-health chatbots, with transparent, checkable verdicts grounded in named rules and facts.

idea.problem: LLM safety evaluations in mental-health contexts lack inspectability and explainability; common approaches (prompt engineering, Constitutional AI) are opaque.
idea.approach: Clinicians define safety rules formally verified for consistency; guardrail layer checks LLM outputs against rule base, with all verdicts traceable to named rules and extracted…
idea.result: Verification layer produces recomputable, transparent judgments; measured disagreements with LLM-as-Judge localize to specific rules and facts; trade-offs quantified on over-…

papers.title: Governed Self-Evolution for Autonomous Investing: A Multi-Agent LLM System with an Invariant Core
papers.abstract: LLM agents that act on live Web data must combine heterogeneous evidence, remember what they have done and improve from outcomes without weakening their own safeguards. We study this problem in autonomous investing, where every action is irreversible and based on untrusted Web content. We present Steward, a multi-agent LLM system that draws the boundary of self-evolution in its type system. First, nine role-specialised agents decide jointly: four analysts read news feeds, SEC filings, macroeconomic series and market data and emit typed reports, from which a Portfolio Manager sets target positions that a protected Risk Manager audits. Second, a seven-layer shared memory, assembled by code from the system's own record, gives each decision its position context, the market narrative, calibration and the agent's past decisions. Third, the system improves itself by review: code grades every trade and forecast nightly and writes the grades into memory, and each quarter a reflector proposes prompt learnings that a deterministic gate applies reversibly and replay of recorded inputs verifies. All three operate around an invariant core of order arithmetic, risk rules and discipline-agent prompts that no self-edit can reach. In a five-month live deployment (102 trading days, 1,632 LLM calls), the system contained a 24.6% sector drawdown to a 0.3% loss; in replay of its recorded inputs, a single model given the same raw data traded more and lost 1.35 points against the market over five days where the joint design showed no significant loss, and no injected instruction was followed; and a 2015-2026 backtest shows the core alone lowering the maximum drawdown under all 50 random entry policies. The reflector traced the dominant failure to its root cause, and the gate applied a learning that the agent adopted on trigger evenings and on no control evening. Code: https://github.com/yebof/quant-agent
papers.why: Multi-agent system with formal safeguards: invariant core that cannot be edited, deterministic gates for self-modification, and runtime verification of agent actions against trading rules.

idea.problem: LLM agents acting on live data must improve without weakening safeguards, especially in irreversible financial decisions
idea.approach: Multi-agent system with protected invariant core (order arithmetic, risk rules), deterministic gates controlling self-edits, shared memory with decision context, and nightly…
idea.result: Live deployment contained 24.6% drawdown to 0.3% loss; single model on same data lost 1.35 points; core alone reduced max drawdown across 50 policies

papers.title: Measuring the Permission Gate: A Stress-Test Evaluation of Claude Code's Auto Mode
papers.abstract: Claude Code's auto mode is the first deployed permission system for AI coding agents, using a two-stage transcript classifier to gate dangerous tool calls. Anthropic reports a 0.4% false positive rate and 17% false negative rate on production traffic. We present the first independent evaluation of this system on deliberately ambiguous authorization scenarios, i.e., tasks where the user's intent is clear but the target scope, blast radius, or risk level is underspecified. Using AmPermBench, a 128-prompt benchmark spanning four DevOps task families and three controlled ambiguity axes, we evaluate 253 state-changing actions at the individual action level against oracle ground truth. Our findings characterize auto mode's scope-escalation coverage under this stress-test workload. The end-to-end false negative rate is 81.0% (95% CI: 73.8%-87.4%), substantially higher than the 17% reported on production traffic, reflecting a fundamentally different workload rather than a contradiction. Notably, 36.8% of all state-changing actions fall outside the classifier's scope via Tier 2 (in-project file edits), contributing to the elevated end-to-end FNR. Even restricting to the 160 actions the classifier actually evaluates (Tier 3), the FNR remains 70.3%, while the FPR rises to 31.9%. The Tier 2 coverage gap is most pronounced on artifact cleanup (92.9% FNR), where agents naturally fall back to editing state files when the expected CLI is unavailable. These results highlight a coverage boundary worth examining: auto mode assumes dangerous actions transit the shell, but agents routinely achieve equivalent effects through file edits that the classifier does not evaluate.
papers.why: Evaluates a deployed permission system for AI coding agents, stress-testing its guardrails against deliberately ambiguous authorization scenarios and measuring coverage gaps.

idea.problem: Claude Code's auto mode permission system has undocumented coverage gaps in guarding dangerous tool calls
idea.approach: Stress-test with AmPermBench benchmark spanning ambiguous DevOps scenarios with controlled risk axes
idea.result: 81% false negative rate on scope-escalation; 36.8% of state-changing actions bypass classifier via file edits instead of shell

papers.title: TrustedCode: Evaluating Large Language Models for Developing Trusted Code through Automated Program Verification
papers.abstract: Recent reports, such as "Who is using AI to code?", indicate that approximately 30\% of Python code contributions to GitHub are AI-generated. Given the inherent unreliability of this code, formal verification emerges as a promising approach to establish trust in software correctness. Although leveraging large language models (LLMs) for formal verification has garnered increasing attention, practical adoption remains limited due to the challenges in writing formal specifications and verifying program correctness against them. Existing tools predominantly support verification for languages such as Java and C, with minimal support for Python. We present TrustedCode, an automated framework for verifying AI-generated Python code. TrustedCode uses LLMs to (i) type-check Python code, (ii) translate it into WhyML via the Why3 framework, and (iii) verify it against formal specifications using Why3 back-end automated theorem provers. Our method integrates chain-of-thought prompting through LangGraph to identify and address LLM limitations in specification generation and proving the specified programs. To evaluate TrustedCode, we conducted experiments on ten Python programs of varying complexity. Our analysis reveals that 50\% of the observed errors stem from domain knowledge gaps, 30\% from syntactic inaccuracies, and the remaining 20\% from semantic and type-related issues. These findings underscore the importance of targeted improvements in LLM-guided formal verification workflows for Python. TrustedCode is an open source tool available at: \href{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}{github.com/mtaimoorkhan/TrustedCode}. The video demonstration is available at: \href{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}{youtu.be/Nr5I2g8ec-s}
papers.why: Automated framework translating Python code to formal specifications (WhyML) and verifying against them using theorem provers, addressing autoformalization and specification challenges.

idea.problem: AI-generated Python code lacks formal verification; existing tools have minimal Python support
idea.approach: LLMs type-check Python, translate to WhyML via Why3, verify with automated theorem provers using chain-of-thought
idea.result: 50% errors from domain gaps, 30% syntactic, 20% semantic; identifies key LLM limitation categories

papers.title: The End of Consensus Research?
papers.abstract: Consensus is a fundamental problem in distributed computing and at the core of state machine replication (SMR). Despite decades of active human research, discovering practical low-latency solutions to the problem is still open, as it requires combining protocol knowledge, correctness reasoning, implementation, and experimental evaluation. We report on how AI helped us discover A-greement, a new consensus protocol for geo-replicated state machines that significantly outperforms state-of-the-art solutions.
