Averaged across six deployments with 5 or 9 replicas, A-greement reduces the mean latency of a geo-distributed key-value store over the fastest baseline by 12.2% and 33.3% on write-heavy and read-heavy workloads, respectively, and matches the fastest baseline on read-only workloads. A-greement combines lease-authorized local reads, direct client learning for leader-ordered writes, and a fast fixed-quorum per-key write path, selected according to network topology and workload. At the heart of our discovery lies AI-greement, an agent harness for the "autonomous" discovery, implementation, experimentation, and verification of candidate protocols. AI-greement integrates (1) a concept-oriented protocol knowledge base, (2) a modular implementation skeleton, and (3) a Lean-based verification framework with reusable safety definitions, reference specifications, and proofs. AI-greement is of independent interest: its Lean formalization uncovers several previously unreported vulnerabilities in existing consensus protocols, and it provides guidelines on how domain-specific harnesses can turn general-purpose coding agents into effective tools for (distributed) computing research. Yet we argue that human consensus experts remain essential before, during, and after the search: agents reshape the researcher's role rather than end consensus research.
papers.why: Presents AI-greement, an agent harness integrating protocol knowledge bases, modular implementations, and Lean verification to autonomously discover and verify consensus protocols, combining formalization and harness design.

idea.problem: Discovering practical low-latency consensus protocols requires integrating protocol knowledge, correctness reasoning, implementation, and evaluation
idea.approach: Domain-specific agent harness combining concept-oriented knowledge base, modular implementation skeleton, and Lean-based verification with reusable…
idea.result: Discovered A-greement protocol reducing geo-distributed latency by 12.2%–33.3% over baselines; uncovered vulnerabilities in existing protocols

papers.title: Validating Autoformalized Specifications via Contrapuntal Languages
papers.abstract: Formal specifications can make AI-generated code mechanically checkable. Because user intent is typically expressed in natural language rather than formal logic, specifications must first be derived from it, e.g., via LLM-based autoformalization. Yet autoformalized specifications are themselves untrusted, so a key challenge is validating whether they capture user intent without relying on a costly oracle such as human review. In this oracle-free setting, a natural strategy is to vote among model outputs, but because model errors are often correlated, agreement among outputs may reflect shared mistakes rather than correctness. Our key insight is that these errors can be decorrelated through representational diversity. We achieve this diversity with contrapuntal languages: pairs of task-specific formal languages, each designed to express the intended specification, yet admitting no structure-preserving translation between them. An LLM formalizes the intent independently in each language, and we accept a specification only if a solver proves the two formalizations equivalent. To construct such languages, we present a synthesis algorithm that reuses fragments of sampled seed specifications as syntactic sugar over a base specification language. We implement the approach for first-order logic specifications and evaluate it on HumanEval+ and LiveCodeBench using GPT-5.4 mini and Qwen3.6-Flash with and without thinking. Over the strongest baseline, our method increases the proportion of accepted specifications that are correct, i.e., complete and sound, by 12.0% on HumanEval+ and 42.9% on LiveCodeBench. The accepted specifications judged complete reject 98.6% of buggy program variants on HumanEval+ and 96.2% on LiveCodeBench, compared with 92.8% and 78.3% for the strongest baseline.
papers.why: Proposes a method to validate LLM-autoformalized specifications by checking equivalence across contrapuntal formal languages, decorrelating model errors through representational diversity.

idea.problem: Autoformalized specifications are untrusted; validating them without human review is difficult because model errors are correlated.
idea.approach: Formalize intent independently in pairs of task-specific formal languages with no structure-preserving translation, then check solver-proven equivalence.
idea.result: 12% and 42.9% improvement in correctness proportion over strongest baseline on two benchmarks; accepted specs reject 96-98.6% of buggy programs.

papers.title: HGM-Dual: Lineage-Aware Guided Agent Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Planning
papers.abstract: Harness optimization, which improves an agent's prompts, tools, and workflows, is an increasingly effective way to enhance agents built on frozen or closed-source LLMs. Leading approaches such as the Darwin--Godel Machine and the Huxley--Godel Machine (HGM) rely on recursive self-improvement and were developed mainly for coding, where the competence needed to improve the agent coincides with the competence being improved. Planning tasks, in which an agent must produce a sequence of tool calls that jointly satisfies interacting constraints, break this alignment. There, open-ended self-modification repeatedly explores ineffective changes and consumes substantial evaluation budgets. We introduce HGM-Dual, a diagnostic-guided framework for budget-efficient harness evolution for planning agents. First, HGM-Dual represents agent evolution as lineage-aware context. This context records what each ancestor changed, which behaviors improved or regressed, and which modifications were ineffective, giving the editor explicit edit-outcome attribution instead of an unstructured archive of past agents. Second, HGM-Dual introduces error-conditioned dual-path child generation. For each selected parent, it generates a general child that preserves open-ended exploration and specialized children that target the harness components most likely responsible for the parent's highest-ranked constraint violations. HGM-Dual outperforms the strongest baseline by up to 14.45% relative improvement in case accuracy while matching HGM variants' final performance with 2x-4x fewer evaluation budget.
papers.why: Proposes a harness optimization framework for LLM-based planning agents that improves prompts, tools, and workflows through structured evolution with diagnostic guidance and constraint targeting.

idea.problem: Planning agents need efficient harness optimization within tight evaluation budgets while balancing exploration and targeted fixes.
idea.approach: Lineage-aware context tracking edit outcomes plus error-conditioned dual-path generation targeting constraint violations.
idea.result: 14.45% relative improvement in case accuracy with 2x-4x fewer evaluations than baselines.

papers.title: PAUSE: Search-Free Steering of Coding Agents Before Their First Source-Code Edit
papers.abstract: Coding agents can invest substantial effort in repository exploration and testing yet still produce unsuccessful patches. Existing online steering methods review trajectories periodically or invoke an advisor when a monitor detects behavioral problems; frequent reviews are costly, and the absence of anomalous behavior does not mean that an agent is on the right track. We propose PAUSE, a framework for steering coding agents with a single planning intervention. Agents reach their first source-code edit at a median of 60% of trajectory progress, after exploration, bug reproduction, and testing. PAUSE intercepts this edit request before it executes, which requires no learned monitor, no search over checkpoints, and no extra model call (search-free). A separate Planner reads the task and the pre-edit transcript and writes one repair plan; the same agent, the Executor, resumes with this plan, keeping its context and workspace. PAUSE applies online, during a live run, and offline, from a recorded trajectory prefix. We evaluate PAUSE on SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Multilingual with two Executors and three agent harnesses. With Qwen3-coder as Executor and GPT-5.6 Sol as Planner, online steering improves resolution by 16.8% on Verified in OpenHands and by 14.7% on Multilingual in SWE-agent. In SWE-agent, PAUSE outperforms LivePlan, a rule-triggered advisor, by 3.2% on Verified and 3.7% on Multilingual at similar Planner cost, and is comparable to SICA's periodic overseer at about 11-15% of its Planner cost. Offline, PAUSE recovers 35.4% of eligible failed Verified tasks, and resuming from the recorded prefix uses 33-41% fewer Executor tokens than restarting.
papers.why: Proposes PAUSE, a framework to steer coding agents before their first code edit by intercepting at a critical decision point, using external planning guidance to constrain agent behavior.

idea.problem: Coding agents explore repositories extensively but still produce unsuccessful patches despite no obvious behavioral anomalies.
idea.approach: Intercept agent at first source-code edit request; external Planner reads task and transcript, writes repair plan; Executor resumes with plan guidance.
idea.result: 16.8% improvement on SWE-bench Verified with online steering; recovers 35.4% of failed tasks offline with 33-41% fewer tokens.

papers.title: Harness Scaling for Generalizable Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses have become a central component of modern agentic systems, shaping how models use tools, manage context, and coordinate long-horizon interaction. Realizing the benefits of these harnesses depends on how effectively the underlying model can make use of them, motivating reinforcement learning directly through the harness. However, existing approaches typically train through a single fixed harness, which can lead to specialization and limited transfer across harness configurations. To address this, we introduce \textbf{Harness Scaling}, a new scaling dimension for agentic RL that extends training from a single harness to diverse execution configurations. Concretely, we construct a factorized harness space, select a compact training subset with balanced factorial coverage, and organize cross-harness training to combine global coverage with controlled variation for the same task. Across multiple benchmarks, model scales, and RL algorithms, Harness Scaling consistently improves generalization to unseen white-box configurations. Moreover, models trained through structured white-box variation transfer effectively to unseen external black-box harnesses, outperforming models trained through a single complex black-box harness. These results establish harness diversity as a meaningful scaling dimension for agentic RL and highlight the importance of how this diversity is organized for cross-harness generalization.
papers.why: Proposes training methods to improve how LLM agents generalize across different harness configurations, directly addressing agent harness design and structured agent scaffolding.

idea.problem: Models trained on single harnesses specialize and fail to transfer to different harness configurations
idea.approach: Introduce Harness Scaling: construct factorized harness space, select compact training subset with factorial coverage, organize cross-harness RL…
idea.result: Models trained through diverse harnesses generalize better to unseen white-box and black-box harness configurations

papers.title: VERDICT: Multi-Agent Parallel Modular Verification
papers.abstract: Deductive verification scales to large software systems through modular reasoning, where formal contracts summarize the behavior of individual functions and enable their independent verification. Its central bottleneck is specification synthesis: constructing the contracts required for modular verification. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated specification synthesis at unprecedented scale. However, existing approaches remain fundamentally bottom-up, requiring callees to be verified before their callers. This dependency limits parallelism and provides no principled mechanism for resolving interprocedural inconsistencies that propagate across call chains. We present VERDICT, a multi-agent framework for parallelizing modular deductive verification of large-scale programs. VERDICT is built on two key principles. First, assumption-based parallel specification synthesis assigns an agent to each function and allows it to proceed immediately using assumed contracts for its callees, enabling verification to proceed in parallel across the program. Second, bidirectional interprocedural conflict reconciliation resolves the inconsistencies introduced by these assumptions: when a synthesized contract contradicts an assumption, agents propagate the necessary revisions both up and down the call graph until the contracts converge. Experimental results on real-world C programs show that VERDICT synthesizes higher-quality specifications than existing approaches while substantially reducing verification time. In particular, VERDICT is the first approach that scales to the complete 20,000-line X.509 parser, ruling out nearly all the potential runtime errors within hours, whereas prior tools like PREGUSS fall far short even after days of execution.
papers.why: Multi-agent framework for parallel specification synthesis and verification through LLM-based contract generation and coordinated conflict resolution across function call graphs.

idea.problem: Specification synthesis bottleneck in deductive verification scales poorly due to sequential bottom-up dependencies
idea.approach: Multi-agent framework with parallel assumption-based synthesis and bidirectional interprocedural conflict reconciliation
idea.result: Scales to 20K-line programs, synthesizes higher-quality specs than existing approaches with reduced verification time

papers.title: AutoFraming: Synthesizing Dynamic Frames of C Code with LLMs
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown considerable promise in synthesizing formal specifications from source code. However, existing approaches primarily focus on functional contracts and loop invariants, while largely neglecting frame conditions, which specify the memory locations that may or may not be modified during execution and constitute an essential part of formal specifications. To address this limitation, we propose an LLM-based approach for synthesizing ACSL frame specifications alongside functional contracts from C code. Our approach analyzes code property graphs (CPGs) to extract frame-relevant information from the input code and leverages this information to guide the LLM in generating accurate frame conditions. The resulting specifications capture both region-separation constraints and data dependencies that govern variable modifications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. On a benchmark of 84 ACSL-compliant functions from non-trivial real-world systems, our method successfully synthesizes error-free frame specifications for 92.9% of the functions, representing a 179% relative improvement over state-of-the-art techniques. On a second benchmark consisting of 51 functions, the success rate increases from 80.4% to 96.1%. Furthermore, when integrated as an auxiliary component into existing LLM-based ACSL-synthesis frameworks, our approach improves frame-specification generation performance by up to 61.9%.
papers.why: Proposes an LLM-based approach to automatically synthesize formal frame specifications (memory modification contracts) from C code, extracting and formalizing implicit behavioral specifications.

idea.problem: LLMs neglect frame conditions when synthesizing formal specifications from C code
idea.approach: Analyze code property graphs to extract frame-relevant information and guide LLM generation of ACSL frame specifications
idea.result: 92.9% success rate on benchmark, 179% improvement over state-of-the-art

papers.title: Semantic Deception: When Reasoning Models Can't Compute an Addition
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in situations where human values are at stake, such as decision-making tasks that involve reasoning when performed by humans. We investigate the so-called reasoning capabilities of LLMs over novel symbolic representations by introducing an experimental framework that tests their ability to process and manipulate unfamiliar symbols. We introduce semantic deceptions: situations in which symbols carry misleading semantic associations due to their form, such as being embedded in specific contexts, designed to probe whether LLMs can maintain symbolic abstraction or whether they default to exploiting learned semantic associations. We redefine standard digits and mathematical operators using novel symbols, and task LLMs with solving simple calculations expressed in this altered notation. The objective is: (1) to assess LLMs' capacity for abstraction and manipulation of arbitrary symbol systems; (2) to evaluate their ability to resist misleading semantic cues that conflict with the task's symbolic logic. Through experiments with four LLMs we show that semantic cues can significantly deteriorate reasoning models' performance on very simple tasks. They reveal limitations in current LLMs' ability for symbolic manipulations and highlight a tendency to over-rely on surface-level semantics, suggesting that chain-of-thoughts may amplify reliance on statistical correlations. Even in situations where LLMs seem to correctly follow instructions, semantic cues still impact basic capabilities. These limitations raise ethical and societal concerns, undermining the widespread and pernicious tendency to attribute reasoning abilities to LLMs and suggesting how LLMs might fail, in particular in decision-making contexts where robust symbolic reasoning is essential and should not be compromised by residual semantic associations inherited from the model's training.
papers.why: Analyzes LLM reasoning limitations through controlled experiments probing symbolic abstraction and semantic robustness, revealing that models over-rely on surface-level semantics rather than performing true symbolic reasoning.

idea.problem: LLMs claim reasoning ability but may exploit learned semantics rather than manipulate symbols abstractly
idea.approach: Test LLMs on arithmetic with redefined symbols designed to create misleading semantic associations
idea.result: Semantic cues significantly deteriorate performance on simple tasks, showing over-reliance on surface semantics over symbolic logic

papers.title: AgentPolicyForge: From Executable Environments to Policy Benchmarks and Adaptive Guards
papers.abstract: Customized agent deployments define policies over tools, resources, and execution conditions. Providing these policies in the task agent's prompt does not reliably prevent violations. Training a guard requires examples of tool calls that comply with or violate those policies. We introduce AgentPolicyForge, a framework that uses executable environments to construct policy benchmarks and iteratively train policy guards. With this framework, we construct PolicyGym, a dataset across ten policy families using 698 scenarios for training data generation and 254 separate held-out scenarios for human-reviewed test sets. Tool calls are executed and their outcomes recorded to help determine whether they comply with the policy. Every violating case uses a permitted tool, requiring checks of arguments, resources, and context rather than tool identity alone. The case construction process supports iterative guard training: an attacker generates requests using retrieved strategies, and the guard is fine-tuned on balanced, environment-verified examples. Training improves policy enforcement even with a fixed archive. Updating the archive further reduces in-domain attack success compared with keeping it fixed. We compare policy-aware task agent self-regulation with a trained policy guard. On PolicyGym, the final guard-based configuration achieves a 40-44% relative reduction in attack success rate and fewer benign rejections than policy prompting alone.
papers.why: Proposes a framework for constructing policy benchmarks and training policy guards to enforce executable policies on LLM-agent tool calls, with specification-based constraint verification.

idea.problem: Prompt-based policies do not reliably prevent agent policy violations; need trained guards to enforce tool call constraints.
idea.approach: Execute tool calls in environments to verify compliance; iteratively train policy guards on balanced, environment-verified examples using adversarial strategies.
idea.result: Policy guards achieve 40-44% relative reduction in attack success with fewer benign rejections than prompt-based policies alone.

papers.title: PerMIT: Securing Persistent Memory for LLM Agents via Machine-Checked Integrity Theorems and Scalable Community Trust
papers.abstract: Persistent memory is a largely undefended surface for injection and poisoning, and the same risk limits memory sharing among agents. We present PerMIT, a memory architecture with provable integrity guarantees under an explicit trust assumption: only user-typed inputs and values confirmed at a gate are trusted. PerMIT mediates the release and use of untrusted environment-derived values through a finite memory interface, while preserving agent-driven multi-turn planning and tool choice. Over this finite interface, we prove two integrity theorems that are also machine-checked in Lean 4, which together ensure that environment-derived memory reaches a sensitive action only if confirmed at the gate and influences the agent's behavior only through what the gate displays. Every attack in our threat model thereby reduces to a single auditable decision, which a human, an LLM verifier, or both can make in practice. On Trojan Hippo, PerMIT records zero observed attack success with self-verification and lightweight verifiers. Because each confirmation is a logged verdict on exact content, endorsements accumulate across users, and sufficiently endorsed items become community-confirmed with no further verification required. Under explicit assumptions, we prove and corroborate in simulation a co-scaling property: as the community grows, the risks of promoting poison and of wrongly evicting benign knowledge fall, while per-user verification effort does not rise. On $τ^2$-bench, communities of up to 90 autonomous agents use PerMIT to build shared knowledge bases with no direct memory injection promoted, and the resulting knowledge significantly improves new agents on held-out tasks, suggesting a path toward agents that safely self-improve at test time.
papers.why: Proposes PerMIT, a memory architecture with machine-checked integrity theorems in Lean 4 that constrains LLM agent behavior by mediating untrusted memory through a gated interface and verifiable confirmations.

idea.problem: Persistent memory is undefended against injection, poisoning, and unsafe sharing among agents
idea.approach: Memory architecture with machine-checked integrity theorems in Lean 4; gates untrusted values; accumulates community endorsements
idea.result: Zero attack success on Trojan Hippo; scalable community verification; improved knowledge base sharing among agents

papers.title: How Much Does the Harness Matter, and for Whom? A Multi-Model Study of Context in LLM-Driven Vulnerability Discovery
papers.abstract: How much does an agent harness affect vulnerability discovery, and does its value depend on the model? We study 24 model-runner configurations using an open-source harness on a production codebase whose vulnerabilities were non-public at scan time. The pipeline combines static screening, LLM investigation, model self-revalidation, root-cause mapping, independent source review, and isolated proof-of-concept confirmation. Across 265 confirmed security root causes, the largest two-run configuration covers 60.4%, while 14.3% are found by exactly one model. No single configuration covers all observed findings. In a four-model context experiment, moving from a minimal prompt to an engineered prompt with a CodeQL-derived call graph raises criticality-weighted yield by 20-86% for smaller and mid-tier models, compared with 2% for the frontier model. This comparison changes both prompt and context. Separating those effects shows that the engineered prompt improves yield for all four models, while adding CodeQL context beyond that prompt improves yield only for the smallest model. A held-out CyberGym subset shows the same direction of target-recall improvement for the combined treatment. Frontier models achieve low false-report rates but do not consistently achieve the highest yield. Strong lower-cost models can deliver similar performance at an order of magnitude lower cost. These results support matching models, prompts, and context to the task, and combining configurations for broader coverage.
papers.why: Studies how agent harness design (prompts, context, component pipeline) affects LLM-driven vulnerability discovery across models, demonstrating that harness engineering significantly impacts agent performance.

idea.problem: Understanding how much agent harness design affects vulnerability discovery across different LLM models
idea.approach: Empirical study of 24 model-runner configurations with varying prompts and context (CodeQL call graphs) on production codebase
idea.result: Engineered prompts and CodeQL context improve smaller-model yield 20–86%; frontier models achieve low false-report rates but not consistently highest yield; combining…

papers.title: An Explicit Feedback Contract for Iterative ML-Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: Iterative ML agents develop models by editing code, running experiments, reading a validation score, and choosing what to try next. In current harnesses this loop is served by an exact validation score returned after every attempt, which leaves the validation split open to adaptive selection. In this work, we introduce an explicit feedback contract for ML-agent harnesses, which specifies what an agent may observe, when iteration should stop, and when the test split may be touched. The contract releases a validation score only when a submission clears a noise threshold computed from the paired standard error, so no margin has to be tuned. We ran experiments on click-through-rate prediction, learning to rank, and a control task with no signal to find. The control is the sharpest case, because the true gain there is zero by construction: an agent reading exact scores ended by reporting a gain of 0.0157, while under the contract it reported 0.0033. On both real tasks the contract narrows the validation-test gap, and test performance is slightly higher rather than lower. The largest difference is in when the agents stop. Exact feedback used its entire budget of thirty submissions on two of the three tasks, including the one where nothing can be learned, while the contract halted after four to twelve. A run that exhausts its budget is usually read as diligence. It is better read as a symptom: when the feedback channel is unbounded, noise keeps supplying improvements to chase.
papers.why: Proposes an explicit feedback contract that constrains what ML agents can observe during iteration, preventing adaptive overfitting and enforcing principled halting—a structural guardrail on agent behavior.

idea.problem: ML agents iterating on validation scores enable adaptive selection and overfitting to the validation split
idea.approach: Introduce explicit feedback contract specifying what agents observe and when to stop, releasing validation scores only above noise threshold
idea.result: Contract reduces validation-test gap, lowers false gains on control task, and causes agents to halt earlier rather than exhaust budget

papers.title: MAS-Guard: Unified Guardrails from Individual Agents to Multi-Agent LLM Systems
papers.abstract: Agentic AI extends large language models (LLMs) from generating responses to planning and executing complex workflows, substantially expanding their utility while exposing applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation. Multi-agent systems further expand these capabilities through specialization and collaboration, but distributed authority, heterogeneous roles, and opaque or potentially compromised participants make safeguarding even more challenging. Existing defenses address important individual threats but provide fragmented coverage across local execution, system-level interactions, and enforcement mechanisms. We introduce MAS-Guard, a unified framework that closes this gap for safeguarding single- and multi-agent AI applications containing both instrumentable and opaque agents. Within instrumentable agents, the proposed local Agent Guardrail (A-Guard) layer applies task-specific experts to assess agentic events. At the system level, developer-owned Agent Charters and a Control Plane combine deterministic structural checks of routes, agent capabilities, and message formats with semantic assessments of roles and message content. These complementary layers enable enforcement through a shared set of interventions: allow, reflection, confirmation, and block. Evaluated across six benchmarks covering diverse single- and multi-agent scenarios with three agent LLMs from different providers, MAS-Guard reduces the overall attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% relative to unguarded agents, while meeting the utility reference criterion on benign tasks.
papers.why: Proposes a unified framework of local and system-level guardrails with enforcement mechanisms to constrain single- and multi-agent LLM systems against unsafe actions and adversarial manipulation.

idea.problem: Multi-agent LLM systems expose applications to unsafe actions, information leakage, and adversarial manipulation across distributed, heterogeneous…
idea.approach: Unified framework combining local Agent Guardrail layer with system-level control plane using structural checks and semantic assessments, enabling allow/reflect/confirm/block…
idea.result: Reduces attack success rate by 71.5-86.3% across six benchmarks while maintaining utility on benign tasks

papers.title: Object-Oriented Harness: Evolving Agent Harnesses through Object-Oriented Design
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses are executable code that specifies the prompts, tools, and control flow around a language model. A single global harness can struggle with heterogeneous tasks that require different execution strategies. In this work, we introduce Object-Oriented Harness (OO-Harness), a harness optimization framework that evolves a hierarchy of executable harness classes using object-oriented design. During training, an evolution agent uses execution records to create a family of specialized harnesses, each implemented as a subclass of the base or an existing specialized harness via inheritance. At test time, a harness router uses routing lessons accumulated during training to select a specific harness for each task. Across three long-horizon benchmarks spanning business workflows, workspace tasks, and tool use, OO-Harness achieves the best performance among the compared methods, with an absolute improvement of up to 15% over the base. Extensive ablation studies examine the contributions of its core components.
papers.why: Proposes a framework for structuring and optimizing LLM-agent harnesses through object-oriented design, enabling task-specific control strategies and routing.

idea.problem: Single global harnesses struggle with heterogeneous tasks requiring different execution strategies
idea.approach: Evolve a hierarchy of specialized harness classes using object-oriented design and route tasks to appropriate harnesses
idea.result: Up to 15% absolute improvement over base harness across three long-horizon benchmarks

papers.title: MaD-RSI: Model-as-Data for Recursive Self-Improvement of Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) of agent harnesses has emerged as an effective approach to enhancing the capabilities of large language model (LLM) agents. By searching the harness space for a specific LLM on a given dataset, RSI can discover a harness tailored to the capabilities and behavioral characteristics of that model. However, such optimization often creates a strong coupling between the learned harness and its target LLM, limiting generalization across models and requiring substantial computational resources to adapt to new LLMs. Moreover, existing RSI methods typically optimize a harness using feedback from a single model and evaluate its generalization to other models only after training. This paradigm treats model differences primarily as a criterion for evaluating generalization rather than as valuable evidence for optimization. In this paper, we introduce a new perspective that treats models as data and places the harness at the center of optimization. Building on this perspective, we propose \textsc{MaD-RSI}, a framework that directly optimizes a shared harness across multiple heterogeneous LLMs by incorporating their diverse failure trajectories into the training process. Rather than assessing model differences only after optimization, \textsc{MaD-RSI} leverages these differences as training evidence to guide the self-improvement of a shared harness. Furthermore, we introduce a new evaluation framework with two complementary metrics designed to assess the effectiveness of harness optimization across models. Experiments across multiple datasets and LLMs demonstrate that \textsc{MaD-RSI} improves generalization over existing approaches while reducing training costs.
papers.why: Proposes MaD-RSI, a framework for optimizing agent harnesses across multiple LLMs by learning from model-specific failure patterns, directly addressing harness design and generalization.

idea.problem: Agent harnesses optimized for one LLM don't generalize to other models and require expensive retraining
idea.approach: Treat models as data; optimize a shared harness by incorporating diverse failure trajectories from multiple heterogeneous LLMs during training
idea.result: MaD-RSI improves harness generalization across models while reducing computational training costs

papers.title: ClawMMU: Protection-Coherent Virtual Memory for Stateful LLM Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents keep long-term memory, much of which comes from web pages and tool results. Agent harnesses, the software that runs the model, do not record who may act on this memory, so an instruction hidden in a fetched page can be treated as the user's own instruction. We propose ClawMMU, a protection layer that labels every piece of memory with its owner, scope, origins, and authority. ClawMMU checks these labels whenever content enters the model's context, is written to storage, returns from storage, or drives a tool call. Its central rule is that information may rise in authority, but authority never lifts itself. Because the checks depend on where content came from, not on what it says, memory attacks become classical protection faults that the harness stops even when the model is fooled.
papers.why: Proposes a protection layer that enforces information-flow control on LLM-agent memory through formal tracking of ownership, scope, and authority labels to prevent prompt-injection attacks.

idea.problem: LLM agents vulnerable to hidden instructions in fetched web pages treated as user commands
idea.approach: Label memory with owner, scope, origins, authority; check labels on context/storage/tool-call boundaries
idea.result: Stops memory attacks as protection faults independent of model fooling

papers.title: A Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning Engine for Compilation-Free Patch Presence Testing
papers.abstract: Code reuse in modern software ecosystems facilitates the spread of 1-day vulnerabilities, posing significant security risks. Determining if patches are present is crucial, but traditional methods suffer from limited usability and accuracy, often depending on a fragile compilation process. In our prior work, we introduced Lares, the first compilation-free framework for patch presence testing that combines large language models (LLMs) with SMT solvers. However, Lares treats the LLM and the SMT solver as two separate, parallel decision channels: the symbolic channel (Z3) succeeded in only 20% of code cases, and the remaining cases fell back to the neural channel (the LLM) for the final decision. Letting the LLM act as the final arbiter turns verification into an informal, non-deterministic process that is prone to hallucination errors, while the two channels never reinforce each other. To overcome these limitations, we propose SyLares, which reformulates compilation-free patch presence testing as neuro-symbolic reasoning. Instead of letting the LLM emit a final verdict, SyLares uses the LLM as a neural feature extractor that perceives heterogeneous source code and decompiled pseudocode and produces specification-compliant SMT-LIB inputs, and delegates the final, deterministic judgment to the symbolic Z3 solver. This neural-perceives, symbolic-decides coupling is realized by a Code2SMT reasoning engine that combines deterministic syntactic parsing with LLM-driven code normalization and symbol alignment, so that every case is reduced to a formal equivalence query rather than an opaque LLM guess.
papers.why: Proposes a neuro-symbolic system that uses LLMs to extract features and generate SMT specifications for patch verification, grounding LLM outputs in formal solvers to replace opaque LLM decisions with deterministic symbolic reasoning.

idea.problem: LLM-based patch presence testing hallucinate; traditional methods lack usability and accuracy
idea.approach: LLM extracts code features and generates SMT-LIB specs; Z3 solver makes final deterministic decision
idea.result: Eliminates LLM as final arbiter, grounds all decisions in formal symbolic verification

papers.title: Local Allow, Global Deny: Why Per-Action Authorization Does Not Compose in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous LLM agents act through tools under per-action authorization: a local guard screens each tool call in isolation. We show that local authorization does not compose into global authorization. A compositional authorization failure (CAF) is a locally authorized execution, or a pair of locally authorized executions, that violates a global policy spanning intent, purpose, provenance, consent, and delegation. We characterize CAFs along two axes, expressiveness (single-trace safety versus relational k-safety) and observability (a ladder of monitor profiles). Our central result is an impossibility: relational purpose violations form a 2-safety hyperproperty with no per-trace locus of blame, so a per-action monitor that never raises a false alarm detects none of them, independent of the underlying model or decision procedure; they become visible only under cross-execution monitoring, which none of the six guardrails we survey implements. We make this constructive with AL-SYNTH, a SAT/SMT synthesizer (using no language model) that emits minimal CAF witnesses, each checked against an exhaustive oracle. The empirical signature is sharp: across nine LLM judges the per-action view approves the synthesized witness almost without exception, blocking it at a rate comparable to a benign control, yet the same models flag it when shown the two executions together. Per-action authorization is therefore structurally insufficient for relational policy conjuncts not reducible to single-trace safety: to bound them, a monitor must compare executions or accept false alarms.
papers.why: Characterizes fundamental limitations of per-action authorization in LLM agents and proposes cross-execution monitoring to enforce relational policies that single-trace monitors cannot detect.

idea.problem: Per-action authorization guards fail to enforce global policies spanning multiple executions or relational properties.
idea.approach: Formalize compositional authorization failures as hyperproperties; synthesize minimal witnesses using SAT/SMT without language models.
idea.result: Relational policy violations require cross-execution monitoring; per-action monitors cannot detect them without false alarms.

papers.title: Act on Your Behalf, Beyond Your Authorization: Benchmarking LLM Agent Authorization Alignment
papers.abstract: When an LLM agent acts on behalf of a user, it is expected to act within the authorization scope the user grants. Existing agent evaluations largely measure task completion or harmful consequences and can therefore overlook actions that violate this delegation without producing conventional safety or privacy harms. We introduce AuthorizationBench, a benchmark of authorization alignment grounded in documented real-world cases. A scalable construction pipeline produces 286 executable tasks spanning situational triggers, the presence or absence of direct harmful consequences, and ten application domains. We execute every task with four models at two reasoning-effort settings across three agent harnesses in an authorization-aware sandbox that keeps authorized and out-of-authorization paths executable and observable, yielding 6,864 trajectories. Agents act out of authorization in 19.2% of trajectories, with rates ranging from 10.5% to 26.6% across the 24 configurations. Task completion does not imply authorization. Increasing reasoning effort leaves the aggregate rate nearly unchanged, with effects varying across models. On controlled pairs, agents act out of authorization at similar rates with (17.9%) and without (20.8%) direct harmful consequences, and more often under benign pressures than malicious injections (23.5% versus 17.6%, p=0.002). Our results show that task capability, additional reasoning, and consequence-oriented safety evaluation do not by themselves ensure authorization alignment. Moreover, agents that consult the principal before completing a task exhibit lower rates of out-of-authorization behavior (14.0% versus 21.6%, p<0.001), pointing to a tension between agent autonomy and preserving users' decision authority that calls for further human-centered study. Dataset and code are available at https://github.com/PEACH-Research-Lab/AuthorizationBench .
papers.why: Introduces a benchmark and evaluation framework for measuring whether LLM agents stay within user authorization scope, with an authorization-aware sandbox and enforcement of delegation boundaries.

idea.problem: LLM agents often act beyond user authorization scope without conventional harms, violating delegation boundaries.
idea.approach: AuthorizationBench: 286 executable tasks across domains with authorization-aware sandbox tracking authorized vs. out-of-authorization paths.
idea.result: Agents act out-of-authorization in 19.2% of trajectories; consultation with principals reduces rate to 14.0%.

papers.title: KNOX: Hardware-assisted Regulatory Sandbox for Generative Models
papers.abstract: Regulations require companies to run AI models in a regulatory sandbox, an isolated environment that enables monitoring model behavior by regulators, prior to deployment. But, they do not spell out the technical mechanisms to design such a sandbox. Ideally, a regulatory sandbox should show (i) compliance (checks against regulations, and deviations from intended behavior, i.e., unauthorized tool and system calls); (ii) confidentiality (protects model weights from regulators); (iii) attestability (produces tamper-resistant evidence of model behavior for monitoring); and (iv) scalability (evidence is verifiable by multiple regulators). Several prior works (information-flow control, prompt-injection defenses, control-flow integrity, and traditional sandboxing) address specific compliance aspects but lack confidentiality, attestability, and scalability. TEEs meet some of these requirements, but simply running models inside a TEE is insufficient as we need compliance mechanisms. We present KNOX, the first regulatory sandbox, built by running AI workloads inside TEEs. We demonstrate KNOX using agentic workloads. For compliance, we derive an attested policy manifest (with the applicable regulations, the expected tool calls, and the permitted system calls) for a given user prompt. Before an executor performs an action, an attested reference monitor compares it against the attested policy manifest and allows it only if it matches. Every action and verdict is recorded in an attested execution graph, enabling regulators to verify the model's execution and its compliance. We show that KNOX meets all requirements, and can check for compliance with regulations and deviations from intended behavior (e.g., due to prompt injection); and incurs low overhead (<1%).
papers.why: Proposes a hardware-assisted regulatory sandbox that enforces compliance guardrails on LLM-agent behavior through attested policy manifests and reference monitors, preventing unauthorized tool and system calls.

idea.problem: Regulatory sandboxes for AI models lack technical mechanisms for compliance monitoring, confidentiality, and tamper-resistant evidence.
idea.approach: Run AI agents in TEEs with attested policy manifests and reference monitors that intercept and verify actions before execution.
idea.result: KNOX sandbox meets compliance, confidentiality, attestability, and scalability requirements with <1% overhead.

papers.title: Harness Self-Evolution for Long-Horizon Terminal Agents
papers.abstract: Long-horizon terminal agents may solve a task in one run yet fail across repeated runs. Stochastic errors can propagate through actions and context, creating a gap between capability and reliable execution. We present RiseHarness, a framework for iteratively improving agent harnesses with model weights fixed. It focuses on flipping tasks with both successful and failed runs under the same configuration, using successful runs as references for failure analysis. RiseHarness combines agent trajectories with internal harness traces from a runtime monitor to examine how model actions interact with command execution, feedback, context management, and completion decisions. A Harness Handbook links this evidence to harness behaviors and source code, helping identify recurring problems in mechanisms shared across tasks. RiseHarness then searches other harness frameworks for relevant implementations and adapts them as design references to the current model and execution protocol. Candidate changes undergo behavioral checks and repeated task evaluation; versions with measured gains seed the next iteration. This loop integrates suitable mechanisms from different frameworks into a single harness and uses new execution evidence to guide further changes. We evaluate task success and reliability across models, ablate harness execution evidence and external research, and test transfer to unseen benchmarks with the same model. RiseHarness treats a specific model as the unit of harness adaptation, studying how changes to shared interaction mechanisms can make existing capabilities more reliable across tasks.
papers.why: Proposes RiseHarness, a framework for iteratively improving agent harnesses through runtime monitoring and constraint adaptation to increase reliability of LLM-agent execution without retraining.

idea.problem: Long-horizon terminal agents fail inconsistently across runs despite having capability, due to stochastic error propagation in actions and context.
idea.approach: Combine agent trajectories with runtime monitor traces to identify harness behavior problems, search other frameworks for solutions, adapt and test candidate harness changes…
idea.result: RiseHarness increases task success and reliability across models; improvements transfer to unseen benchmarks with same model.

papers.title: Toward Safe LLM Agents: A Survey of Specification, Verification, and Enforcement
papers.abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents take irreversible real-world actions, yet no system gives formally grounded, task-level safety guarantees for their plans. In a PRISMA 2020 systematic review, we searched six databases (20-29 May 2026) for work on LLM agent specification, verification, and enforcement published in 2022-2026. We narratively synthesized 38 studies, assessed risk of bias per study, and graded evidence certainty with GRADE. Three authors independently screened a repeated search to validate the single-reviewer screening (agreement: Fleiss' $κ= 0.81$). First, specification is the bottleneck: on one benchmark, only 24.8-34.2% of LLM translations from natural language into Planning Domain Definition Language (PDDL) are semantically correct. Second, runtime monitoring is the most mature enforcement strategy; it reduced unsafe actions by 65.37% in one household-agent study, but its guarantees cover only single steps or short horizons. Third, in one $τ$-Bench study of transactional tool-use agents, blocking 94% of unsafe actions still left fewer than 5% of tasks completed both safely and correctly in most settings, because agents found other unsafe routes (the verifier tax). Fourth, no approach simultaneously achieves soundness, completeness, scalability, semantic grounding, and utility preservation. For seven of the nine principal claims, GRADE gives the lowest certainty rating (Very Low), meaning further studies are likely to produce substantially different figures; each rests on one or two studies in narrow domains. Two of the open problems we rank highest are translating requirements into formal specifications that keep their meaning and enforcing safety over whole plans rather than single actions. We contribute a three-level taxonomy and an agenda of ten open problems.
papers.why: Systematic review of LLM agent specification, verification, and enforcement covering formal specifications, PDDL translation, runtime monitoring, and safety guarantees for agent actions.

idea.problem: LLM agents lack formally grounded safety guarantees; specification, verification, and enforcement methods are immature and fragmented
idea.approach: Systematic PRISMA 2020 review of 38 studies on agent specification, verification, and enforcement from 2022-2026
idea.result: Specification is bottleneck (24.8-34.2% semantic correctness); runtime monitoring most mature but limited to short horizons; no approach achieves all desiderata; ranked open…

papers.title: VerifierBench: Benchmarking the Generation of Executable Verifiers for LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Agents need reliable ways to validate their outputs, both when completing tasks and when filtering synthetic training data. We study verifier generation: from the instruction and environment available for solving a task, an agent writes an executable verifier that must accept every valid solution and reject invalid ones. We introduce VerifierBench, a benchmark of 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks spanning tool-call, state-based, and code verification, with 4,993 hidden test cases that include alternative valid solutions and attacks; Verifier4Verifier (V4V), a six-check audit, screens its source verifiers and test suites. Across 19 models in a common agent harness, normalized balanced accuracy ranges from 10.6 to 62.1, with generated verifiers consistently rejecting invalid solutions more reliably than they accept valid ones. This apparent strength can mask overly restrictive verification: most false rejections in the analyzed records come from verifiers that accept no tested solution to a task. Case studies reveal unsupported assumptions about solution formats, tool use, and code changes that exclude valid solutions. These errors survive self-testing because agents test solutions that share the verifier's mistaken assumptions, or submit verifiers without confirming that any correct solution passes. These findings suggest testing both whether a verifier accepts a correct solution and whether it accepts other solutions permitted by the task. The project page and dataset are publicly available.
papers.why: Introduces a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents' ability to generate executable verifiers that validate task solutions, a key guardrail mechanism for constraining agent behavior.

idea.problem: LLM agents need reliable verifiers to validate outputs and filter synthetic data, but verifier generation quality is unclear and undertested
idea.approach: Create VerifierBench with 222 tasks from six agent benchmarks and 4,993 test cases, including alternative solutions and attacks; use Verifier4Verifier to audit verifiers and test…
idea.result: Verifiers show 10.6–62.1% normalized balanced accuracy; most failures are overly restrictive due to unsupported format assumptions that pass…

papers.title: Same Simulation, Different Evidence: Where Retrieved Tool Output Costs LLM Agents Accuracy
papers.abstract: LLM agents that compute the right answer can still answer wrongly. Agent harnesses increasingly keep long tool outputs out of the context window, saving them to files that the agent searches or reads on demand. We ask where this costs accuracy with a real scientific tool: PHREEQC, a widely used geochemistry simulator from the USGS, whose reports reach 846.8k characters and whose determinism lets every printed value be traced. Agents use it to answer 158 execution-verified multiple-choice items. When agents read the simulator's report through a section index rather than in context, GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2 lose 11.3 and 7.9 points of accuracy, while Claude Opus 4.6 and Claude Sonnet 4.6 show no detectable cost. Re-running all 11,007 logged simulator calls shows that both GPT models compute the keyed value about as often as before; what changes is the evidence they answer from. Under retrieval they often skip the report, answer from their own higher-precision output files, and misround to a neighboring option, a failure we call evidence substitution. With the simulation held fixed, retrieval still costs GPT-5.2 9.4 points. For GPT-5.4, more frequent correct simulations mask an evidence-use loss of about ten points, leaving a net change indistinguishable from zero. Naming the authoritative output raises accuracy by 6.3-7.9 points over plain retrieval for the three GPT models; for GPT-5.1 and GPT-5.2, inlining outputs that fit works as well, while asking for correct rounding does not. Context-management choices in agent harnesses should be judged by where accuracy is lost, not only by final accuracy.
papers.why: Empirically analyzes how agent harness design (context management and tool-output retrieval) affects LLM accuracy, revealing failure modes in evidence use that inform guardrail design.

idea.problem: LLM agents using retrieved tool outputs instead of in-context reports lose accuracy through evidence substitution and misreasoning
idea.approach: Trace all simulator calls and compare agent accuracy with in-context vs. retrieved tool outputs, analyzing where reasoning fails
idea.result: GPT models lose 7.9–11.3 accuracy points under retrieval due to skipping authoritative outputs; Claude models unaffected; naming authoritative outputs recovers 6.3–7.9…

papers.title: When the harness decides success: state that cannot be re-observed
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses decide what a language model sees across turns: they drop old turns, summarize them, or replay the model's own earlier reasoning. We ask when these choices change whether an agent succeeds, not only what it costs, and report three findings. First, in a pre-registered synthetic probe, truncating the context window costs a low-cost reasoning model nothing in success when a needed fact can be looked up again (it looks the fact up instead), but drops its success to chance when the fact cannot be re-observed: the two penalties differ by 92.5 percentage points (90% CI [89.5, 95.5]). A pre-registered replication on one model from a second provider showed the same contrast. Once the fact was lost, that model chose no answer rather than guessing. Second, on ARC-AGI-3, where the benchmark's Standard harness trails its Provider Adapter harness by a wide margin, we decompose that gap one component at a time, for one model on four games. Summarizing old turns instead of dropping them, while keeping the Standard harness's invitation to take notes, recovers 86% of a 63-point gap without replaying the model's reasoning. The same harness without the invitation recovers 43%, and adding the provider's native replay of the model's reasoning recovers the remaining 57%. These are point estimates from one counted run per configuration and game, and the replay share depends on a single run. Third, in the benchmark's published runs and in ours, the Adapter's advantage in the probability of clearing a level it has reached is larger at deep levels than at early ones. This largely restates where runs stopped and does not separate a growing advantage from a constant one.
papers.why: Analyzes how agent harness design choices (context truncation, summarization, memory replay) affect LLM agent success, showing that harness-imposed information constraints determine whether agents can re-observe critical facts.

idea.problem: Agent harnesses control what LLMs see across turns; unclear when design choices change success vs. just cost
idea.approach: Pre-registered experiments measuring agent success under different harness memory/context strategies
idea.result: Context truncation costs nothing when facts are re-observable, but drops success to chance when irretrievable; harness components recover most of performance…

papers.title: VerusEval: Evaluating LLM-Generated Verus Specifications Beyond Verifier Acceptance
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate Verus contracts for Rust programs together with the proofs that establish them. Yet verifier acceptance, the common measure of success, shows only that the implementation satisfies the generated contract, so it leaves open whether the contract captures the intended behavior. Assessing specification generation therefore requires an evaluation methodology, not a single metric. We present VerusEval, a framework that evaluates generated contracts along six dimensions, including Verus-native checks for semantic triviality, validated input-output (I/O) suites, and contract equivalence, and that relates them so that the strength and blind spots of each become measurable. Evaluating 13,716 artifacts from four workflows, five LLMs, and two prompting settings on 762 tasks, we find that acceptance overstates quality: only 42.3\% of the accepted artifacts complete all three semantic checks without a flag, and across workflows and models, higher acceptance does not consistently come with more correct contracts. I/O evaluation rejects 23.6\% of the accepted artifacts, yet only 63.2\% of those that pass it are proved equivalent. Of the accepted artifacts flagged by contract comparison, 84.1\% have a rejected completeness obligation, and the direction of a failure prioritizes inspection of the generated contract or the reference; it does not by itself establish which artifact is defective. Screening and review further identify 36 candidate defects among 61 selected reference contracts, and repairing one of them makes 10 of its 11 failing artifacts equivalent. Based on these findings, we derive four actionable lessons for evaluation, generation, and benchmark maintenance.
papers.why: Introduces a comprehensive evaluation framework for assessing LLM-generated formal specifications (Verus contracts) beyond verifier acceptance, with systematic methodology and large-scale empirical analysis.

idea.problem: Verifier acceptance alone does not guarantee LLM-generated contracts capture intended behavior
idea.approach: Multi-dimensional evaluation framework with six checks: semantic triviality, I/O validation, equivalence comparison, and contract analysis
idea.result: Only 42.3% of accepted contracts pass all semantic checks; acceptance significantly overstates specification quality

papers.title: Reliable Before Profitable: QuantHarness for Governing Financial Strategy Development with LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents can turn natural-language financial research requests into executable and backtested strategies, but a successful run may still implement the wrong rule, use information unavailable at decision time, or obscure how repairs and candidate selection changed the strategy. Because these failures arise throughout development, final code and performance metrics alone are insufficient to establish either fidelity to the request or the validity of the development process. We therefore address the reliability of financial strategy development at the trajectory level: the system must control how intermediate outputs become downstream state and preserve the evidence needed to justify the terminal outcome. We introduce QuantHarness, a two-layer agent harness in which a finance-specific Workflow structures specification, data grounding, construction, testing, and review, while Harness Core enforces stage-specific information, action, and commitment boundaries. We also introduce FinRelBench, a benchmark that evaluates strategy-development reliability through execution success, requirement satisfaction, and runtime evidence. QuantHarness achieves the highest Task Success at 90.72\%, compared with 74.23\%--84.54\% for the comparison systems. Controlled stress tests show that its boundaries contain targeted violations, while structured run records improve evidence retrieval and support decision replay under the evaluated protocol.
papers.why: QuantHarness is an agent harness that enforces stage-specific boundaries and constraints on LLM-agent behavior in financial strategy development, with runtime verification and structured evidence preservation.

idea.problem: LLM agents developing financial strategies may violate requirements, use unavailable data, or obscure the development process despite successful execution.
idea.approach: Two-layer harness with finance-specific workflow and enforcement of information, action, and commitment boundaries at each development stage.
idea.result: QuantHarness achieves 90.72% task success vs 74.23–84.54% for baselines; stress tests verify boundary enforcement and structured records support decision replay.

papers.title: Maestro: Agentic Formal Proof Development by Coordination
papers.abstract: Lean is increasingly used to verify mathematical proofs and software produced by LLM agents, but writing formal proofs remains hard. Existing prover systems take a divide-and-conquer approach that recursively decomposes hard proof obligations into easier lemmas and splits again any lemma that resists proof. However, a lemma can resist proof for different reasons, including insufficient guidance, a false statement, or a flaw in the decomposition that produced it. Existing systems cannot tell these apart as a failed attempt reports little beyond its failure, and responses are confined to the failing node without considering the rest of the proof or revising the plan above it. The system may thus keep decomposing obligations along a flawed proof direction until the budget runs out, causing the whole proof attempt to fail. We introduce Maestro, a Lean prover harness that handles failures through global coordination. Provers report why they failed, not just that they failed, and a coordinator that sees the whole proof chooses an appropriate response, such as guiding a stuck prover, correcting a false lemma, or retracting a flawed subtree and replanning it. The same harness extends to verified code synthesis, where a checked counterexample sends the code back for repair. We evaluate Maestro with four frontier LLMs on seven mathematics and three software verification benchmarks. It proves more targets than each model's native coding agent (Claude Code or Codex) on every benchmark the agent has not already saturated, with the largest gains on research-level mathematics. With Claude Opus 5, it discovers its own proofs of 34 of the 48 theorems in the June 2026 release of arXivLean, against 19 for the native agent. It also outperforms all published prover systems on every benchmark they share, solving 669/672 PutnamBench, 59/60 Lean-IMO-Bench, and 6/6 IMO 2026.
papers.why: Presents Maestro, a Lean prover harness that coordinates LLM agents through structured failure reporting and global replanning to improve formal proof development.

idea.problem: LLM-based provers fail without explaining why, leading to wasted computation on flawed proof directions
idea.approach: Agent harness with rich failure reporting and central coordinator that decides between guiding, correcting, or replanning proof attempts
idea.result: Proves more theorems than native agents on math and software benchmarks; 34/48 arXivLean theorems with Claude Opus

papers.title: Better Specifications, Better Code: Fine-Tuning LLMs for Behavioral Contract Generation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong code-generation capabilities but often struggle with functional correctness due to implicit or ambiguous behavioral requirements. We present CG2, a contract-guided code generation framework that translates natural-language tasks into structured behavioral contracts specifying interfaces, preconditions, postconditions, and invariants. CG2 fine-tunes an LLM to generate these contracts and introduces an iterative semantic validation and repair process to identify and correct incomplete, inconsistent, or incorrect specifications before guiding an unchanged downstream code-generation model. We evaluate CG2 on 1,007 held-out tasks using five code LLMs: DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Lite-Instruct, Ministral-3-14B-Instruct-2512, Qwen2.5-Coder-14B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct, and Qwen3.5-27B. Results show that CG2 consistently improves pass@1 over direct code generation by 1.49-3.27 percentage points (7.58%-22.45% relative improvement) and over contract guidance without fine-tuning by 1.19-2.38 percentage points (7.04%-14.65% relative improvement). Manual analysis further reveals that semantically correct contracts are associated with higher code-generation accuracy. These findings demonstrate that explicitly specifying and validating behavioral requirements can improve functional correctness without modifying downstream code-generation models.
papers.why: Fine-tunes LLMs to generate formal behavioral contracts (preconditions, postconditions, invariants) from natural language to improve code generation and correctness.

idea.problem: LLMs generate code without explicit formal specifications, leading to functional correctness issues from ambiguous requirements
idea.approach: Fine-tune LLM to generate behavioral contracts, then iteratively validate and repair them before using for code generation
idea.result: 7.58%-22.45% relative improvement in pass@1 over direct code generation across five code LLMs

papers.title: Beyond a Single Direction: Chain-of-Thought Disrupts Simple Steering of Refusal
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) generate chain-of-thought (CoT) traces before producing final outputs, introducing a dynamic internal state that may complicate control mechanisms such as refusal. Unlike instruction-tuned LLMs, where refusal is mediated by a single directional subspace, refusal in large reasoning models (LRMs) additionally depends on the CoT. In DeepSeek-R1-Distill-LLaMA-8B, activation steering reverses refusal in only 39% of cases when the CoT is kept fixed, but removing the CoT entirely increases this to 70%, indicating that the CoT actively reinforces refusal. In a two-stage intervention where the model regenerates its CoT under activation steering, refusal is reversed in 94% of cases, while the resulting CoT alone retains 48% of this effect even after steering is removed. This suggests that the CoT can carry and reconstruct the compliance signal independently. These findings indicate that refusal in LRMs is jointly encoded in residual stream activations and CoT. This joint activation makes LRM more robust against activation-level interventions alone, but exposes CoT to a possible alternative surface attack.
papers.why: Analyzes how chain-of-thought reasoning interacts with refusal mechanisms in LRMs through mechanistic interpretability and activation steering interventions.

idea.problem: Activation steering for refusal control fails in reasoning models when chain-of-thought is present
idea.approach: Empirically examine activation steering effects with and without CoT, studying how CoT encodes and reinforces refusal signals
idea.result: CoT jointly encodes refusal with residual streams; regenerating CoT under steering reverses refusal in 94% of cases

papers.title: Symbolic Constraint Agents: Mining Formal Tool-Call Constraints to Prevent Agent Errors
papers.abstract: Symbolic constraints (programmatic, deterministic checks for tool calls) enable deterministic verification of LLM agents' tool calls, but existing approaches primarily enforce predefined safety policies rather than tool dependencies in complex tool environments. We explore whether symbolic constraints can be mined from environments and observations beyond predefined policies, and whether they can improve end-to-end task performance. We present Symbolic Constraint Agents (SCA), a framework that mines symbolic constraints from API documentation, refines them against execution traces, and checks the agent's tool calls with an SMT solver at runtime. A violation triggers a natural-language warning or, when the valid replacement is uniquely determined, an automatic repair. On AppWorld, refinement raises error-detection F1 from 37.0 to 58.3 on GPT-5.5 traces and from 39.3 to 61.9 on Qwen3.5-27B traces. At runtime, repair raises GPT-5.4-mini's task success by 5.4 points under a 40-call budget and 9.8 points when environment errors are hidden, while removing 59--87\% of failed calls across models, and transfers to $τ^2$-bench with gains of up to 5.6 points. These findings show that automatically acquired symbolic constraints can improve tool-calling reliability and task completion, particularly when failures are costly or difficult to diagnose.
papers.why: Mines symbolic constraints from API documentation and traces to enforce tool-call correctness, then uses SMT solver verification and automatic repair at runtime to constrain LLM-agent behavior.

idea.problem: LLM agents make invalid tool calls; predefined safety policies miss tool dependencies in complex environments
idea.approach: Mine symbolic constraints from API docs and execution traces; verify calls with SMT solver; repair or warn at runtime
idea.result: Constraint refinement improves error detection F1 by ~20 points; runtime repair increases task success by 5.4–9.8 points and removes 59–87% of failed…

papers.title: Structure-Aware Equivalence for Evaluating Autoformalized Statements
papers.abstract: Evaluating autoformalized mathematical statements requires determining whether a candidate preserves the mathematical claim intended by a trusted reference. Existing methods approach this problem from complementary directions: reference-free learned evaluators estimate semantic agreement but are not constrained to a formal equivalence relation, while reference-based proof methods typically employ whole-statement logical equivalence to provide formal certificates, which is too coarse for translation fidelity and may identify mathematically unrelated statements. We introduce Structure-Aware Equivalence (SAE), a role-preserving formal equivalence relation between syntactic and whole-statement logical equivalence that allows formally justified reformulations while preserving translation-relevant mathematical structure. We operationalize SAE in the Autoformalization Correctness Evaluator (ACE), which provides certified equivalence or inequivalence judgments and reports Inconclusive otherwise. On ProofNetVerif, a benchmark introduced with BEq+, ACE retains substantial equivalent-case coverage while remaining highly conservative in certifying disputed or inequivalent pairs. On targeted diagnostics, BEq+ accepts 94-96% of unrelated but whole-statement logically equivalent pairs, while Mathesis LeanScorer accepts 42% of localized meaning-changing perturbations; ACE accepts none of either set as equivalent.
papers.why: Proposes Structure-Aware Equivalence, a formal method to evaluate whether autoformalized mathematical statements preserve intended meaning while accounting for legitimate reformulations.

idea.problem: Evaluating autoformalized statements needs to preserve mathematical meaning while allowing legitimate reformulations.
idea.approach: Introduce Structure-Aware Equivalence (SAE), a role-preserving formal relation between syntactic and logical equivalence, operationalized in ACE evaluator.
idea.result: ACE provides certified equivalence judgments while correctly rejecting unrelated logically-equivalent statements where other methods fail.

papers.title: VeGo: Direct Deductive Formal Verification of Go Programs for Computer Science Education
papers.abstract: As formal methods are rapidly becoming accessible and practical due to AI coding agents, priority passes to assisting developers and students in generating specifications. Leveraging native HMX/SSA verifiers provide that support with rigorous mathematical guardrails. We present VeGo (Verified Go), a deductive formal verification system that enables direct verification of standard Go source code. VeGo incorporates Hoare-style contracts, loop invariants and integer variants, well-founded recursive measures, block-level scope invariants, and equational reasoning chains with primed variables directly as non-intrusive Go comments. We detail the language selection rationale justifying Go as an ideal balance over C, C++, Java, and Rust, strategically adopting Go's native multiple return values. We detail the tool architecture, exploiting the theoretical equivalence between Static Single Assignment (SSA) form and first-order functional programming to annotate code, desugar of clopen interval quantifiers, add Reynolds' skip statement, provide weakest precondition calculus, and native Hindley-Milner constraint inference, and verification condition resolution over the SSA form. We formalize contract-precision checking (weakest precondition vs. strongest postcondition) using an explicit analogy to type inference. Finally, we evaluate VeGo across educational textbooks and outline a roadmap for formal concurrency specifications using epistemic temporal logic.
papers.why: VeGo translates Go source code annotated with Hoare-style contracts into formal verification conditions, enabling direct deductive verification with mathematical rigor.

idea.problem: Students and developers need accessible formal verification without intrusive annotations or language changes.
idea.approach: Embed Hoare contracts, loop invariants, and reasoning chains as Go comments, then desugar to SSA form for verification condition generation.
idea.result: Tool that verifies standard Go code with weakest precondition calculus and contract-precision checking; evaluated on educational textbooks.

papers.title: PAAC: Privacy-Aware Agentic Device-Cloud Collaboration
papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents face a structural tension: cloud agents provide strong reasoning but expose user data, while on-device agents preserve privacy at the cost of overall capability. Existing device-cloud designs treat this boundary as a compute split rather than a trust boundary suited to agentic workloads, and existing sanitizers force a choice between policy flexibility and the structural fidelity tool calls require. In this work, we develop PAAC, a privacy-aware agentic framework that aligns planner--executor decomposition with the device-cloud boundary so that role specialization itself becomes the privacy mechanism. The cloud agent reasons over typed placeholder tokens that preserve each sensitive value's reasoning role while discarding its content, while the on-device agent identifies sensitive spans and distills each step's execution outcome into compact key findings. Sanitization confines the on-device LLM to proposing which spans to mask, while a deterministic registry performs all substitution and reversal, keeping actions directly executable on device. On three agentic benchmarks under strict privacy settings, PAAC dominates the Pareto frontier of privacy and accuracy, improving average accuracy by 15-36\% and reducing average leakage by 2-6$\times$ over state-of-the-art device-cloud baselines, with the largest margins on privacy targets outside fixed entity taxonomies. We find consistent improvements on 17 additional benchmarks spanning 10 domains, including math, science, and finance.
papers.why: Proposes a framework for structuring LLM agents across device-cloud boundaries with privacy-preserving guardrails that constrain information flow and sanitize sensitive data before cloud processing.

idea.problem: LLM agents must balance reasoning capability with user data privacy across device-cloud systems
idea.approach: Decompose agent into on-device sanitizer and cloud planner using typed placeholders and deterministic masking registry
idea.result: 15-36% accuracy improvement with 2-6× less data leakage vs. baselines on agentic benchmarks

papers.title: Bellman Language Models: Solving the Recurring Decisions of LLM Agents
papers.abstract: A general observation in agentic workflows, especially bounded ones, is that the decision space of the LLM, when we separate a decision from generation, starts approaching saturation: the agent meets the same states again and again, and after enough conversations it stops meeting new ones. LLMs generally don't treat these decisions as an optimization problem and instead re-derive them from their context/prompt on every turn. We show that treating decision making within reasonable bounds as an optimization problem, solving it once, and reusing the solved decisions can often make an agent faster, cheaper and more reliable. Our approach, which we call Discretize, Then Decide, starts from data such as the workflow's own logs or, when none exists, runs of the LLM agent itself. It reads each conversation into discrete states and estimates the probability of each outcome and the cost of each move, until no new states appear and the probabilities stop changing. It then solves the resulting Markov decision process. The solution runs as a controller around the model, sending moves whose content is fixed in the state, such as a tool call or a templated reply, and any state it hasn't seen is sent back to the LLM. We call an LLM run this way a Bellman language model (BLM), after Richard Bellman's equation for the best move in each state. On $τ^2$-bench telecom, the controller with no model solves 79% of tasks. As a BLM, Qwen3.8-27B, an open model, goes from 29% to 96% with 93% fewer model calls. For Claude Opus 5.5, which solves 96% of tasks on its own, running it as a BLM cuts model calls and cost per task by about 98% and lets it solve 2 more tasks. On InventoryBench, the solved policy with no model beats every published method. Where the hard part is writing content rather than choosing moves, such as resolving SymPy issues, few decisions can be solved in advance, and a BLM helps little.
