papers.why: Proposes a controller harness that learns and reuses decision policies from agent logs, converting recurring LLM decisions into a solved MDP to constrain agent behavior and improve efficiency.

idea.problem: LLM agents re-derive decisions from context repeatedly, wasting compute on recurring states
idea.approach: Extract discrete states and outcomes from agent logs, solve as MDP, deploy solved policy as controller harness
idea.result: 96% task success with 93% fewer model calls for Qwen; 98% cost reduction for Claude while maintaining performance

papers.title: Verifying Human-Written Reasoning References
papers.abstract: Evaluating the reasoning of AI systems often relies on human-written reasoning chains as references, yet the logical support for their individual steps is rarely verified. Although prior neuro-symbolic approaches have formalized and checked reasoning, their reported evaluations do not systematically assess whether step conclusions in human-written reference derivations are entailed by their cited premise sets or investigate the sources of failures in those references. To address these limitations, we present a novel reference-centred assessment method for human-written derivations that combines entailment checking against cited premise sets, full-premise rechecking, and failure attribution to examine the reliability of these derivations and their formal representations. We evaluate it on P-FOLIO, using a large language model (LLM) to translate step conclusions into first-order logic (FOL) and the Z3 SMT solver to check entailment. Of 386 derivations examined, 202 (52.3%) meet all our checking criteria, meaning that every translated step is entailed by its stated support and the required target is established under the available FOL representations. Among 230 steps not entailed by their stated support, 191 become entailed when checked against the complete original premises, indicating that most initial failures reflect incomplete or mismatched support rather than unsupported claims. Manual analysis of the remaining 39 cases identifies 21 human reasoning errors, 11 FOL translation errors, and 7 dataset annotation errors. A separate manual audit of 50 randomly sampled steps that passed the entailment checks found 46 faithful FOL translations (92%). These findings suggest that disagreement with a human-written reasoning reference may originate in the reference or its formal representation rather than in the AI system being evaluated.
papers.why: Systematically evaluates the logical validity of human-written reasoning references using LLM-based FOL translation and SMT solver verification, identifying sources of failures in formal representations.

idea.problem: Human-written reasoning references used to evaluate AI are rarely verified for logical correctness
idea.approach: Translate step conclusions to FOL using LLM, check entailment with Z3 SMT solver, attribute failures to reasoning errors or translation issues
idea.result: 52.3% of derivations fully valid; most failures reflect incomplete premise support rather than unsupported claims

papers.title: Proving LLM-Generated GPU Kernels Correct and Safe: Floating-Point Verification in Lean and VerCors
papers.abstract: Modern statistical model development begins with a high-level specification in an automatic differentiation framework such as PyTorch, JAX, or TensorFlow, which is then lowered to a target backend by a compiler or implemented manually by a research engineer. In this paper, we study whether frontier language models can correctly perform the latter task by generating GPU kernels from high-level benchmark specifications. We introduce a framework in which a language-model agent uses Velvet, a program verifier for imperative programs embedded in Lean, to prove semantic equivalence between a high-level specification and a generated CUDA kernel under an explicit set of assumptions. It also asks the LLM to prove thread safety and data race freedom of the generated kernel in VerCors, a deductive verifier for parallel code. Our main contribution to the formal verification of LLM- generated GPU kernels is showing that a combination of Lean automation and language-model-guided proof construction can verify a broad set of basic neural- network building blocks over floating-point values, allowing LLMs to implement semantically correct and safe kernels. In our framework, floating-point verifications never rely on compiled code and are always checked via the Lean kernel.
papers.why: Builds an agent harness using Lean and VerCors to verify that LLM-generated GPU kernels are semantically correct and safe, combining formal verification with LLM-guided proof construction.

idea.problem: Verifying that LLM-generated GPU kernels match high-level specifications and are thread-safe
idea.approach: Agent uses Lean verifier to prove semantic equivalence and VerCors for thread safety; LLM guides proof construction with automated checking
idea.result: Framework successfully verifies neural-network building blocks over floating-point values with proofs checked by Lean kernel

papers.title: Instruction Self-Arbitration Is Not a Trust Boundary: Configuration-Dependent Tool Calls and External Enforcement in LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents receive instructions from system prompts, users, memory and tools, and labels inside a shared context are not an enforceable trust boundary. We study how measurement and configuration choices change what benign file-deletion tasks on gateway-labelled endpoints appear to show (an availability-selected roster) and test an external reference monitor. The original keyword flag for detecting fabricated authority mostly matched negated phrases: two blind judges flagged the claim as fabricated in at most 1 of 150 GPT-4.1-mini responses. In a fully logged reflection re-run, responses that both express doubt and delete are rare after a reflection instruction (25 of 509 executions), and a casual request that gives a reason but claims no authority is executed by all ten endpoints. Source-format cues are linearly decodable (97.5-100% probe accuracy, four open-weight models), but a pre-specified crossed-probe test halted and gives no interpretable evidence of an abstract provenance representation, and steering did not move tool mention (0 of 1,895 trials, mention-scored). On the same 14,294 diverse-prompt trials across 29 endpoints, the rule fixed before collection gives an endpoint mean of 1.21%; a path-based reading chosen after the data were seen gives 12.9% [6.6-20.1%, 29 models]; any delete call gives 20.2%. In 1,350 sandbox trials, all 750 forged, tampered, replayed and unsigned records were rejected at admission and no file outside a token's scope was removed (a functional-correctness test, not a robustness estimate). Semantic authorisation remains open: a deputy with a valid scoped token induced in-scope deletions in 31/42 trials, and legitimate privileged requests produced at least one in-scope deletion in 120/150 (144/150 and 36/42 with a larger output limit).
papers.why: Empirically evaluates external reference monitors and runtime enforcement mechanisms for constraining LLM agent tool calls against instruction injection and unauthorized actions.

idea.problem: LLM agents cannot enforce trust boundaries on tool calls through instructions alone; malicious or confused directives can cause unintended actions.
idea.approach: Deploy external reference monitors and sandbox enforcement to validate agent tool calls against permission rules and detect forged or unauthorized requests.
idea.result: External monitors reject forged/tampered records but semantic authorization remains hard; instruction labels alone are not a reliable trust boundary.

papers.title: NeurOWL: An LLM-Based Neural-symbolic Framework for Incomplete OWL Ontology Reasoning
papers.abstract: OWL ontologies provide a formal knowledge representation framework that enables semantic reasoning, and have been widely adopted across domains such as healthcare and bioinformatics. In practice, however, real-world ontologies are often incomplete, which pose challenges for reasoning. In this work, we focus on a fundamental subsumption reasoning problem: given an incomplete ontology and a candidate (non-entailed) subsumption, determine whether the subsumption is semantically plausible and, if so, providing a logically sound explanation containing potential missing axioms. This task unifies subsumption verification with ontology abduction, and generalizes the latter by removing the need for a predefined candidate set of missing axioms. To address this subsumption reasoning problem, we propose NeurOWL, an end-to-end neuro-symbolic framework that jointly performs verification and abduction, leveraging both formally defined semantics and textual semantics through Large Language Models and ontology embeddings. We evaluate NeurOWL on real-world ontologies across multiple domains, demonstrating strong and robust performance across different domains.
papers.why: Combines LLMs with formal ontology reasoning (OWL) to verify subsumption claims and generate missing axioms, bridging natural and formal semantics for incomplete knowledge representation.

idea.problem: Real-world OWL ontologies are incomplete, making subsumption reasoning unreliable and requiring missing axiom discovery
idea.approach: Neuro-symbolic framework combining LLMs, ontology embeddings, and formal OWL semantics for joint verification and abduction
idea.result: Strong performance on subsumption verification and plausible axiom generation across real-world ontologies in multiple domains

papers.title: Janus: a Playground for User-Involved Agentic Permission Management
papers.abstract: AI agents that autonomously execute tool calls on a user's behalf raise pressing questions about permission management: what role could users play, and what role should they play? Despite many proposed approaches, the user's role in agentic permission management remains underexplored. We introduce Janus, a playground system for implementing and evaluating user-involved agentic permission management designs. Janus consists of two components: Janus-Core, a modular agentic system supporting a diverse spectrum of permission management designs, and Janus-Harness, an automated evaluation framework. Grounded in a conceptual model that identifies key design axes for user involvement, we implement six permission assistants spanning the design space and evaluate them across three scenarios with four subscenarios each and three synthetic responders. We demonstrate that user involvement is critical and can strengthen privacy and security and that user behavior such as permission fatigue must be accounted for in system design. No single design performs optimally across all contexts, motivating a more principled and context-sensitive approach to deploying permission assistants in agentic systems. Janus is publicly available to support future investigation into this dimension of agentic system design.
papers.venue: 48th IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy
papers.why: Provides a playground system for designing and evaluating permission management harnesses that constrain LLM-agent tool calls through user involvement and formal permission models.

idea.problem: Users lack control over what tools AI agents autonomously execute on their behalf
idea.approach: Modular agentic system with permission assistants spanning user-involvement design space and automated evaluation framework
idea.result: User involvement strengthens security; no single design optimal across all contexts

papers.title: RATION: Towards Quantitative Risk-Based Access Control for AI Agents
papers.abstract: AI agents increasingly interact with external environments to complete complex user tasks. These interactions can lead to unexpected behavior and expose agents to security threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current agent security systems largely protect agents by restricting their actions, which can result in a substantial security-utility trade-off for complex, open-ended tasks. To address this, we propose a quantitative risk-based approach to access control for AI agents that regulates measurable risks accumulated during task execution. As a concrete realization of this approach, we introduce RATION, a security framework that tracks measurable risks associated with agent actions and enforces quantitative constraints throughout execution. RATION first constructs a task-specific policy by combining explicit constraints derived from the user request with implicit risks calibrated from historical executions of similar tasks. During task execution, RATION continuously tracks the accumulated risks and applies different enforcement strategies depending on the type of risk. Extensive experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION provides strong security while maintaining high task utility across diverse models and environments.
papers.why: Proposes RATION, a quantitative risk-based access control framework that enforces guardrails on AI agent actions during execution by tracking measurable risks and applying constraints.

idea.problem: AI agents face security threats like prompt injection while maintaining task utility; restrictive access control hurts complex tasks.
idea.approach: Track measurable risks from agent actions using explicit constraints and implicit calibration from historical tasks; enforce quantitative constraints during execution.
idea.result: Strong security with high task utility across four benchmarks and diverse models.

papers.title: SPIDES: Information-Flow Control for Browser Agents
papers.abstract: Browser agents automate complex workflows by reading and acting on arbitrary page content, but this flexibility exposes them to prompt injection attacks and unintended data exfiltration. Recent work argues that LLM-driven browser agents erode traditional web security boundaries such as the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) by acting across origins with the user's authority and no built-in isolation. We argue that restoring SOP is neither sufficient (a same-origin public sink can leak private data) nor necessary (legitimate tasks require authorized cross-origin flows) for protecting the security of users. We propose SPIDES, which instead enforces information-flow control by gating primitive browser actions such as typing, clicking and navigating on labels propagated from element-level HTML confidentiality and integrity annotations. Untrusted and confidential content is masked from the agent's context, while policies block unauthorized flows, providing security guarantees against both prompt injection and data exfiltration that hold independently of the model driving the agent. To evaluate SPIDES and baseline defenses under a common threat model, we build MicroNet, a closed ecosystem of 28 interlinked websites with element-level ground-truth labels and paired benign/adversarial tasks. SPIDES achieves 0% attack success rate by design while retaining high task completion rate and autonomy. Our findings demonstrate that information-flow control is an effective technique to extend web security to browser agents, gaining on autonomy and utility against state-of-the-art baselines. The source code and data are openly accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/SPIDES.
papers.why: Proposes information-flow control as a logic-based guardrail to constrain LLM browser agents, enforcing security policies on primitive actions through element-level labels independent of the model.

idea.problem: Browser agents expose users to prompt injection and data exfiltration by acting across origins with user authority
idea.approach: Enforce information-flow control via labels on HTML elements, gating browser actions like typing and clicking
idea.result: Achieves 0% attack success rate while maintaining high task completion and autonomy compared to baselines

papers.title: DrugHarness: An Evolvable Agent Harness for Computational Drug Discovery
papers.abstract: Computational drug discovery requires agents to compose scientific operations and adapt to changing evidence and constraints. Here we introduce DrugHarness, an evolvable agent harness coupling composable scientific execution with conditional skill induction. Its environment integrates over 80 scientific operations, biomedical resources and task-specific code, preserving associations among candidates, results and artifacts. From execution trajectories and outcome feedback, DrugHarness induces action hypotheses with observable applicability conditions, recommended actions and supporting evidence. An independent review agent evaluates candidate skills derived from these hypotheses through source verification and, when needed, targeted execution trials. Admitted skills guide subsequent tasks and are revised through feedback. Evaluation on MolBench and SMDD-Bench demonstrates capabilities in molecular screening, optimization and constrained design. Without evolution, DrugHarness exceeds reported MolClaw-CC results by 10.8 percentage points in affinity-comparison accuracy and 55% in mean top-three active hits on MolBench. Retrospective evaluation on skill-development tasks shows that evolution increases Qwen's affinity-comparison accuracy from 62.2% to 81.1% and optimization success from 79.5% to 87.2%. In a prospective HPK1 study, DrugHarness achieves a more favorable median docking score than Biomni among system-specific candidates. A synthesized compound achieves a cellular IC50 of 14.19 nM, a 2.64-fold potency improvement over the best input reference, with activity competitive with two selected compounds designed by experienced medicinal chemists. These results support conditional skill evolution for scientific agents and demonstrate a workflow connecting computational drug design with experimental validation.
papers.why: Presents an agent harness for drug discovery that structures agent behavior through composable operations, skill induction with observable conditions, and independent verification—exemplifying guardrails and control mechanisms around scientific agents.

idea.problem: Computational drug discovery agents must compose scientific operations and adapt to changing constraints and evidence.
idea.approach: Harness integrates 80+ scientific operations with conditional skill induction, outcome feedback, and independent review verification of learned skills.
idea.result: Exceeds baselines on MolBench; skill evolution improves affinity-comparison accuracy from 62.2% to 81.1%; prospective HPK1 study yields 2.64× potency improvement.

papers.title: MuninAI: A Self-Hosted Agentic Framework for Independent Research Groups
papers.abstract: Research groups that want a language model grounded in their own literature face a choice between hosted services that receive their unpublished work and self-hosted deployments that keep the data local but give the model no access to the corpus. Munin is an open-source framework for a self-hosted scientific assistant that indexes a group's corpus and its citation graph, and wraps whichever open-weight model the group can serve in an agent harness with specialised reading, search, and computation tools. We claim that the harness, rather than the specific model, is what makes the system useful on domain literature, and we ship the evaluation suite that tests this claim with the software. On 199 paired literature questions, the harness more than doubles the accuracy of the base model, from 0.387 to 0.874 (+0.487, 95% CI [0.407, 0.568]), while naive retrieve-then-answer scores below the unaided model on every backbone tested. Under the harness, roughly twice as many answer claims trace to a passage the model read itself as with fixed top-5 retrieval. When the source paper for a question is removed from the corpus, the system abstains on about nine in ten of the questions it had answered correctly on the Qwen backbones and eight in ten on gpt-oss-20b, and it produces no fabricated local citation across 300 fabricated references. The pattern holds on three backbones from two developers, including a 20-billion-parameter model that runs on a single consumer-grade GPU. With all outbound network access disabled, both Qwen backbones still exceed the published PaperQA2 accuracy. The evaluation suite runs as a single command, so an adopting group can re-run it on its own corpus and model.
papers.why: Self-hosted agentic framework with specialized tools, guardrails against hallucination, and evaluation of agent behavior on domain tasks without data exposure.

idea.problem: Research groups need local LLM access to their corpus without sending unpublished work to hosted services.
idea.approach: Self-hosted agent harness wrapping open-weight models with reading, search, computation tools and citation grounding.
idea.result: Harness doubles base model accuracy to 0.874; traces 2× more claims to read passages; abstains when source missing; no fabricated citations.

papers.title: GatewayBench: Unified Capability and Security Evaluation Platform for MCP Gateways
papers.abstract: AI agents have increasingly interacted with external environments by invoking tools, with Model Context Protocol (MCP) emerging as a standard interface for connecting agents to heterogeneous tools and services. As organizations deploy agents at scale, MCP gateways have become a critical middleware layer for aggregating, governing, and shaping the tool surface exposed to agents. Despite the growing importance of MCP gateways in agentic systems, no prior work has systematically studied how gateway design affects agent capability, efficiency, and security. To address this gap, we introduce GatewayBench, the first unified evaluation framework and benchmark for MCP gateways. We characterize gateway architectures into two major paradigms: flattened gateways and hierarchical gateways. GatewayBench comprises 524 tasks across six domains, together with a pool of 11,118 real-world tools from 251 authentic MCP servers. To emulate large-scale deployments, we systematically inject task-irrelevant tools sampled from this pool into each agent environment, enabling controlled evaluation as the accessible tool surface scales. Based on GatewayBench, we conduct extensive experiments across seven widely deployed MCP gateways and diverse agent configurations, covering both benign and adversarial tasks. Our results reveal substantial differences across gateway designs in task completion, tool-use efficiency, and resilience to attacks, and further demonstrate that these effects interact strongly with the underlying model and agent harness. These findings highlight the MCP gateway as a consequential yet underexplored component of the agentic AI stack. By enabling controlled evaluation of gateway architectures under realistic tool ecosystems, GatewayBench provides both practical guidance for MCP gateway design and a rigorous testbed for developing more capable, efficient, and secure agentic systems.
papers.why: Introduces a benchmark framework for evaluating MCP gateways as a guardrail layer controlling tool access, capability, and security in LLM-agent systems.

idea.problem: MCP gateways govern agent tool access but lack systematic evaluation of their design impact on capability, efficiency, and security.
idea.approach: Create GatewayBench with 524 tasks across six domains, 11,118 real-world tools, and controlled injection of task-irrelevant tools to evaluate seven gateway architectures.
idea.result: Substantial differences in task completion, tool-use efficiency, and attack resilience across gateway designs; effects interact with model and agent harness.

papers.title: Monitor-Validity Failures: LLM Safety Evidence Paths at Evolving Framework Boundaries
papers.abstract: Modern LLM applications rely on runtime monitors that inspect tool calls, traces, streams, detector outputs, and verifier inputs. This creates an interface-reliability problem: a framework path may remain operational while policy-relevant evidence never reaches its decision point. In one representative case, a regex detector returned a positive match, but the framework stranded the result before the block decision. This differs from jailbreaks and detector errors because the evidence is already recognized yet disconnected from enforcement. We study this repair-boundary signature with canary contracts: parent/fixed confirmation units that place a known payload only on the changed evidence surface and record monitor visibility together with the downstream decision for action-boundary cases. Applying the protocol to public framework repairs, we confirm 18 evidence-path failures across 11 LLM or agent safety project groups and four implementation ecosystems. Nine are established-boundary repairs, eight are new-surface policy-coverage gaps, and one is a boundary-only evidence case. Fourteen reach E1 enforcement boundaries: seven native action outcomes, six configured enforcement boundaries, and one synthetic-consumer consequence. The remaining cases affect verifier, safety-prompt, or observability channels. The cases form carrier, adapter, authority, and surface families and show how ordinary application behavior can remain intact while a safety-specific evidence path misses its decision. Exact revisions, deterministic outcomes, negative controls, and a frozen prospective audit document the confirmation rule. Monitor assumptions therefore need regression tests at the schemas, streams, tools, and adapters that frameworks evolve.
papers.why: Empirical study of runtime monitoring failures in LLM agents, identifying and categorizing evidence-path disconnections where safety monitors fail to enforce policies despite detecting violations.

idea.problem: LLM agent safety monitors detect policy violations but fail to enforce them due to framework structural issues
idea.approach: Canary contracts to trace evidence paths through framework boundaries and identify where violations disconnect from enforcement decisions
idea.result: Found 18 evidence-path failures across 11 projects showing monitor visibility problems at framework boundaries

papers.title: Towards Agentic Proof Harness Engineering
papers.abstract: Formal verification of real-world projects requires substantial manual effort, from specifying correctness properties to constructing the infrastructure needed to check them. We envision verification agents that assist developers throughout this process. Among the many tasks involved, one stands out as both foundational and amenable to automation: proof-harness engineering. A proof harness defines an isolated verification environment for a program unit, such as a function or module, by providing symbolic inputs, initialization code, and models of its dependencies. Today, proof-harness engineering remains largely a manual task performed by verification engineers. To explore the potential of coding agents for this task, we propose an agentic proof-harness engineer that automatically constructs verifier-ready harnesses from a software project and a designated verification target. We combine the agent with formal soundness and precision guards to validate generated abstractions and guide their refinement. We evaluate the feasibility of our approach in an exploratory case study on curl and libuv, using three historical assertion violations already embedded in the source code as verification properties. Our results show that the agent successfully constructs proof harnesses that enable CBMC to detect all three violations. We further demonstrate the potential for reusing these harnesses with other verification tools.
papers.why: Proposes an LLM agent that automatically constructs formal verification harnesses with soundness guards, combining agent scaffolding with formal verification infrastructure.

idea.problem: Manual proof-harness engineering for formal verification is tedious and error-prone
idea.approach: LLM agent that generates harnesses from code, validated by formal soundness and precision guards
idea.result: Successfully detects three historical assertion violations in curl and libuv using CBMC

papers.title: Towards Agentic Cloud Engineering: Graph and Loop Engineering with a Zero-Trust Agent Harness
papers.abstract: Agentic AI is enabling cloud-based workflows in which autonomous agents reason over operational state, invoke authorized tools, modify software and infrastructure, deploy services, verify execution outcomes, and adapt across long-horizon, multistep tasks. Engineering such workflows requires explicit mechanisms for workflow progression, constrained execution, failure recovery, and verifiable completion. We present Agentic Cloud Workflow Engineering, an agentic AI framework that transforms natural-language agentic cloud-engineering tasks into validated code repositories and verified operational cloud deployments for automating cloud-based agentic workflows. The framework separates three complementary concerns: graph engineering specifies long-horizon workflow progression and verification-dependent transitions; loop engineering provides bounded diagnosis, repair or re-planning, retry, and re-verification; and agent harness engineering enforces zero-trust execution through identity, authorization, policy-scoped capabilities, isolation, and runtime safeguards. Workflow progression and completion require machine-checkable repository, deployment, and runtime evidence, with recovery constrained by explicit operational bounds and termination criteria. We instantiate the framework on Google Cloud and evaluate repository completeness, controlled execution, evidence-gated progression, operational deployment, and bounded recovery. Experimental results show that executions terminate with either a verified operational cloud deployment or an auditable terminal failure under bounded recovery. The framework provides a unified engineering architecture for cloud-based workflows spanning Agentic DevOps, Agentic CloudOps, Agentic SRE/AIOps, Agentic SecOps, Agentic DataOps, Agentic MLOps/LLMOps, AgentOps, Agentic RAG/GraphRAG, and related cloud-engineering domains.
papers.why: Proposes a zero-trust agent harness framework with explicit mechanisms for constrained execution, authorization, policy enforcement, and runtime safeguards to control LLM-agent behavior in cloud workflows.

idea.problem: Agentic AI workflows need explicit constraints, verification, and safety mechanisms for autonomous cloud operations
idea.approach: Framework separating graph engineering for progression, loop engineering for bounded recovery, and harness engineering for zero-trust execution with identity and policy…
idea.result: Executions terminate with verified deployments or auditable terminal failures under bounded recovery on Google Cloud

papers.title: Evaluating the Robustness of Proof Autoformalization in Lean 4
papers.abstract: Proof autoformalization aims to translate a mathematical informal proof in natural language into a formal proof in a formal language such as Lean 4. Existing LLM-based models for proof autoformalization are typically evaluated only on well-formed informal proofs from curated datasets. We argue that a robust proof autoformalizer must remain faithful even for informal proofs that diverge from these idealized ones, and we present the first study on the robustness of proof autoformalization models. We formulate two categories of perturbations: a global perturbation paraphrases the informal theorem-proof pair in a different style, under which the formalization should remain consistent; a local perturbation alters a value, symbol, or proof step, possibly in a counterfactual way, and a robust formalization should faithfully reflect the perturbation rather than reverting to the original or inferring a different one on its own. We build a benchmark with both perturbations on miniF2F and MATH-500, and automatically measure how stable a proof autoformalization's correctness is under global perturbations and how faithfully its output reflects local perturbations. We evaluate seven recent models: their correctness varies under global perturbations, and they mostly fail to remain faithful under local perturbations.
papers.why: Introduces a benchmark with perturbations to evaluate robustness of LLM-based proof autoformalization models translating natural-language proofs into Lean 4.

idea.problem: LLM proof autoformalizers are only evaluated on curated proofs; robustness to variations is unknown
idea.approach: Create benchmark with global and local perturbations to test stability and faithfulness of formalizations
idea.result: Seven models show varying correctness under global perturbations and mostly fail local perturbation faithfulness

papers.title: Language Models as Higher-Order Planning Formalizers
papers.abstract: Recent work provides overwhelming evidence that LLMs, even those trained to scale their reasoning trace, quickly deteriorate at planning as problems become more complex. LLM-as-Formalizers aim to address this by employing LLMs as a bridge to translate natural language descriptions into structured planning representations such as PDDL, which are then fed to a programmatic solver. We observe that its success may be overstated because planning problem descriptions in standard benchmarks often have a one-to-one mapping to PDDL, which departs from real use cases. To address this, we introduce the notion of unraveling problems where a natural yet succinct description translates into a very large PDDL representation. Using unraveling variants of four standard planning domains, we demonstrate that LLM Formalizers also do not always scale. We tackle this challenge by introducing a new paradigm, LLM-as-Higher-Order-Formalizer, where the LLM generates a high-level program that captures the recurrent logic within the description and in turn generates the larger PDDL representation. This decouples token output from the combinatorial explosion of the underlying formalization and search space, leading to improved performance for complex problems.
papers.why: Proposes using LLMs to translate natural language planning descriptions into formal PDDL representations, with a novel higher-order approach to handle complex problems that require large formalizations.

idea.problem: LLMs fail at complex planning; standard benchmarks have one-to-one natural language to PDDL mapping, unlike real use cases with large formalizations
idea.approach: Generate high-level programs capturing recurrent logic that then produce PDDL, decoupling token output from combinatorial explosion
idea.result: Higher-order formalizer improves performance on complex planning problems with unraveling variants

papers.title: Model-as-a-Trojan: Self-Activating Covert DNS Exfiltration Baked Into the Weights of an LLM Agent
papers.abstract: Open-weight models are downloaded from public hubs and run inside agent harnesses that grant them tools, most powerfully, a shell, under the assumption that a sandbox contains whatever the model might do. This paper demonstrates that the assumption has a blind spot: the weights themselves can be the malware, and the sandbox's last open door, DNS, is enough. We fine-tune an open-weight LLM so that a single covert behavior lives in its parameters: on the first turn of every conversation, whenever the model infers from its context that a shell tool is available, it emits one self-contained command that reads a secret from the runtime environment, base32-encodes it, chunks it, and exfiltrates it as DNS queries toward an attacker-controlled authoritative name server. It then answers the user normally and never mentions, or repeats, the act. Because the channel is DNS, the attack completes from inside a container with no internet egress beyond name resolution - measured payload-level and model-level behind an egress firewall that drops every non-DNS packet, with the secret reconstructed from the gateway resolver's query log. Because the behavior lives in the weights, prompting is the only off-switch a victim has, and it is unreliable: the implant fires in 20/20 of adversarial suppression trials, deflects direct interrogation without disclosing the sequence, and sweeps a 45-cell sandbox-fault matrix across five tool-calling formats - plus a fresh post-training canary, persona-only and absent system prompts, and an egress-locked topology - with zero leaks and zero repeat fires. Every training trajectory is execution-verified in a real container, and every claimed exfiltration is proven resolver-side: we reconstruct the secret from the authoritative resolver's query log alone.
papers.why: Demonstrates a critical vulnerability in LLM agent harnesses where malicious behavior encoded in model weights can bypass sandbox defenses and evade detection, highlighting the need for stronger agent guardrails and monitoring.

idea.problem: LLM agents in sandboxes with tool access can harbor malicious behavior in their weights that evades detection and sandbox constraints.
idea.approach: Fine-tune an open-weight LLM to embed covert DNS exfiltration behavior triggered by shell tool availability, then test evasion across sandbox configurations and suppression…
idea.result: Malicious implant successfully exfiltrates secrets via DNS from inside containers with no internet egress, survives all suppression attempts (20/20), and maintains stealth across…

papers.title: Repairing LLM-Generated Specifications with Deterministic Diagnosis
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as formalizers: given a reasoning problem expressed in natural language, they produce a formal specification that a symbolic solver can then solve, with guarantees relative to that specification. Many specifications are runnable yet semantically wrong, encoding incorrect constraints, domains, objectives, predicates, or goals, and solver-error feedback dries up once execution succeeds. Purely LLM-based diagnosis, lacking a formal ground truth, often fails to spot these errors, and its ungrounded critiques cause regressions in 11.8% of initially correct specifications in our experiments. We propose DRAGO, a repair framework that replaces this ungrounded critique with deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis, and retains a rewrite only when the diagnosed error weight strictly decreases under a reference-free acceptance predicate. Across five benchmarks spanning logical reasoning (SMT-LIB2), constraint programming (MiniZinc), and planning (PDDL), DRAGO cuts regressions by nearly an order of magnitude, to 1.3%, while improving answer accuracy by 12.9 percentage points over zero-shot formalization and 8.7 percentage points over LLM-diagnostic repair, averaged across benchmarks. We also uncover two rendering defects in Planetarium that cause 50% (3,086 instances) of its floor-tile split to be inconsistent with the reference formalizations, and release a corrected split.
papers.why: Proposes DRAGO, a framework using deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis to repair LLM-generated formal specifications (SMT, MiniZinc, PDDL) rather than ungrounded LLM critique.

idea.problem: LLM-generated formal specifications are semantically wrong despite executing, and LLM-based diagnosis causes regressions
idea.approach: Use deterministic, formalism-specific diagnosis with reference-free acceptance predicates to repair specifications
idea.result: DRAGO reduces regressions to 1.3% and improves answer accuracy by 12.9 points over zero-shot formalization

papers.title: Harness-Delta Attribution: Dissecting Gains From Harness Evolution
papers.abstract: Harness evolution automatically optimizes the prompts, skills, tools, and orchestration code around a fixed-weight model, offering a way to improve agentic systems without updating model weights. The agent harness is iteratively optimized to achieve higher performance on the search set. But how much of this gain reflects benchmark-specific overfitting or additional inference-time compute, and how much may generalize beyond the search set? In this work, we introduce Harness-Delta Attribution (HDA), an evaluation protocol that dissects an evolution gain into artifact-driven overfitting, gains explained by test-time scaling, and the remainder, which gives an upper bound on residual generalizable improvement. We apply HDA to 11 executor models and three harness-evolution frameworks across math, coding, creativity, and agentic tasks. In 21 of these settings that show statistically significant search-set gains, we find that a large share of the improvement is explained by overfitting or test-time scaling. Specifically, among these 21 settings, overfitting and test-time scaling account for 54% and 14% of the gain on average; their combined share exceeds 50% in 14 settings. The residual and held-out transfer vary substantially across tasks, models, and frameworks. Importantly, search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks, and provide limited evidence that they will persist under practical distribution shifts. Moreover, validation-based signals are insufficient to prevent overfitting. These results motivate attribution-aware evaluation in future harness evolution research.
papers.why: Evaluates harness-evolution frameworks for LLM agents, analyzing overfitting and generalization in prompts, skills, and orchestration—core to understanding and improving agent harness design.

idea.problem: Harness evolution gains are not attributed; unclear how much is overfitting vs. generalizable improvement
idea.approach: Harness-Delta Attribution protocol dissects gains into overfitting, test-time scaling, and residual improvement across models and tasks
idea.result: 54% overfitting and 14% test-time scaling on average; search-set gains often fail to transfer to held-out tasks

papers.title: From Natural Language Intent to Executable Control: Hierarchical Feedback-Guided LLM Planning for Multi-component Cyber-Physical Systems
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide a convenient interface for translating natural language commands into task plans for cyber-physical systems (CPSs). However, two gaps hinder their use for real execution: generated plans may misinterpret or omit the user's intent, and even a logically plausible plan may be infeasible under component dynamics, interactions, or safety constraints. Existing LLM-based planning approaches often lack informative feedback on why a generated plan fails, providing little guidance for revising the plan accordingly. To address these challenges, we present a hierarchical feedback framework that uses different types of feedback information to guide LLMs in generating executable plans for CPSs. We prompt LLMs to generate both a structured task plan and corresponding signal temporal logic (STL) constraints, and design a sound algorithm that identifies definite contradictions between them and provides feedback for revising inconsistencies. At the execution level, when control synthesis fails, we extract different types of diagnostic information, such as violated constraints and conflicting component assignments, and feed them back to guide task replanning. Experiments on seven heterogeneous multi-component CPS scenarios have shown that our framework can generate executable plans and feasible control executions that satisfy the original natural language missions with a success rate of 87.9% with GPT-5.
papers.why: Translates natural language commands into formal STL constraints for cyber-physical systems with structured feedback loops and runtime verification to ensure plan feasibility and safety.

idea.problem: LLM-generated plans for cyber-physical systems may misinterpret intent or violate safety/dynamics constraints without informative feedback.
idea.approach: Hierarchical feedback framework using STL formalization, contradiction detection, and execution-level diagnostics to guide LLM replanning.
idea.result: 87.9% success rate on multi-component CPS scenarios in generating executable plans satisfying missions.

papers.title: My Credentials, Please: Detecting Filesystem Capability Laundering in MCP Servers at Scale
papers.abstract: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) standardizes how AI agents invoke external tools. MCP servers expose tools through a declared contract consisting of a name, description, and argument schema. In typical local deployments, client-side approval of a tool call grants the underlying server process broad host filesystem permissions rather than restricting it to the declared operation. We study the resulting vulnerability class, filesystem capability laundering, where attacker-steered arguments cause a tool to access sensitive host files outside its declared contract and deployment scope. We analyze this capability gap across three layers: server-category screening (L1), per-tool contract analysis (L2), and bypassable path-validation checks (L3). We design MCP-FSD to catalog MCP servers, infer least-privilege boundaries per tool, plant credential fixtures outside those boundaries, and evaluate exploitability and sandbox containment via paired dynamic execution. Across 21,097 MCP servers from nine registries, 787 of 4,806 triaged servers (16.4%) exhibit filesystem capabilities despite non-filesystem functional classifications. Dynamic three-case validation confirms 150 vulnerable instances under tested sandbox policies. Coordinated disclosure yielded 13 security advisories, including two CVEs in Anthropic's Git MCP Server.
papers.why: Identifies and evaluates a capability-gap vulnerability in MCP agent tool invocations, proposing multi-layer guardrails and sandbox enforcement to constrain agent filesystem access to declared tool contracts.

idea.problem: MCP agent tool calls grant broad filesystem permissions beyond declared contract scope
idea.approach: Multi-layer analysis (screening, contract, validation) with dynamic exploitation and sandbox containment testing
idea.result: 16.4% of MCP servers exhibit undeclared filesystem capabilities; 150 vulnerable instances confirmed

papers.title: PROBE: Learning to Audit Policy Compliance in Tool-Using LLM Agents
papers.abstract: Modern agentic systems extend language models with external tools, enabling them to complete complex tasks through multi-turn interactions. As these agents are deployed in consequential settings, they are often constrained by policies governing pricing, privacy, confirmation, safety, and other requirements. However, existing evaluation methods leave a critical gap: capability benchmarks measure what agents can accomplish, while content-safety red-teaming measures harmful generations, but neither tests whether agents comply with predefined policies during otherwise valid tool use. Such policy violations are difficult to audit because their effects may emerge only after several turns, span multiple tool calls, or surface in downstream systems. We propose PROBE (Policy Rule Observation via Behavioral Exploration), an algorithm for training LLM-based auditors that interact with deployed agents as realistic users and probe them for policy violations through multi-turn, tool-mediated dialogue. We formalize agent auditing as a two-player Markov game and propose a composite reward that balances violation discovery, behavioral plausibility, conversation progress, and policy diversity. To study training objectives and reward design, we compare GRPO, DPO, and GFlowNet-based optimization in a controlled setting. Across extensive experiments, auditors trained with PROBE uncover substantially broader and higher-yield policy violations than same-architecture zero-shot adversaries, even when the auditor is significantly smaller than the target agent. Our results show that multi-turn behavioral auditing is a distinct and necessary axis of agent evaluation, complementing capability and safety benchmarks. PROBE offers a scalable path toward automated policy auditing for real-world agentic systems and suggests a co-evolutionary loop in which auditors expose failures and agents improve from auditor feedback.
papers.why: Proposes PROBE, an algorithm for training LLM-based auditors to detect policy violations in tool-using agents through multi-turn interactions, exemplifying runtime monitors and specification-based constraints for agent behavior.

idea.problem: Agentic systems with tools lack systematic auditing for policy compliance across multi-turn interactions and tool calls
idea.approach: Train LLM auditors using RL (GRPO, DPO, GFlowNet) to interact with agents as users and probe for policy violations via realistic dialogue
idea.result: PROBE auditors discover substantially more violations than zero-shot baselines, enabling scalable automated policy auditing for deployed agents

papers.title: DeciCAD: Harness-Grounded Learning of Action Policies for CAD Agents
papers.abstract: Large Language Model agents operate through closed-loop action policies whose decision space is defined by an agent harness. We investigate how this operating space shapes agent behavior and policy learning in computer-aided design (CAD), a professional domain characterized by persistent state, geometric constraints, and long-horizon procedures. We instantiate this perspective in DeciCAD, a domain-native harness that exposes semantic CAD actions, decision-oriented observations, environment feedback, and persistent state transitions. Building on this harness, we develop a learning pipeline that extracts causal decision supervision from interaction trajectories and improves the policy through supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and geometry-grounded online reinforcement learning (RL). Across four CAD benchmarks, DeciCAD achieves the best F1 and intersection over union (IoU) while reducing model-output tokens by 45--88% relative to a general-purpose coding harness. Under matched supervision, its SFT policy improves F1 from 0.6883 to 0.7437 and outperforms the coding policy; subsequent online RL further raises geometry availability from 66.5% to 73.5% and F1 to 0.7880. These results demonstrate that the decision space induced by a harness materially affects both agent execution and policy learning in CAD.
papers.why: Proposes DeciCAD, a domain-native agent harness that structures LLM-agent behavior in CAD through semantic actions, observations, and state transitions, with learning techniques grounded in this harness design.

idea.problem: LLM agents need structured operating spaces tailored to complex domains like CAD with persistent state and geometric constraints
idea.approach: Design domain-native harness exposing semantic CAD actions and geometry-grounded feedback; extract causal supervision from trajectories; use SFT and geometry-grounded…
idea.result: Harness design improves F1 from 0.69 to 0.79 with RL, reduces output tokens by 45-88% versus general coding harness

papers.title: DialFork: Going Beyond Factuality to Evaluate Procedural Hallucination in Conversational Agents
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as conversational agents are increasingly expected to follow procedural logic. While factual hallucination has received extensive attention, a different failure mode has been overlooked: procedural hallucination, in which an agent produces individually fluent and factually plausible utterances while deviating from the intended conversational process. We introduce DialFork, the first benchmark to measure this failure mode on raw dialogue text. DialFork is built by forking conformant dialogues at controlled turn positions and injecting one of four hallucination types, yielding 36,278 dialogues across 24 tasks in 12 domains; 30 human annotators validate the construction. We define three evaluation tasks that characterize procedural deviation at three granularities: how far a set of dialogues deviates from conformant ones (monitoring deployed agents), how far a single dialogue does (procedural retrieval), and at which turn a dialogue first goes off-track (real-time guardrails). For the first two, we propose dialog-flow-aware metrics, FlowKL and FlowScore, that compare dialogues by how they unfold rather than their content. At the dialogue level, FlowScore significantly outperforms all baselines across seven encoders, showing that semantic similarity is no substitute for procedural similarity. We release DialFork under the MIT license at https://github.com/idiap/dialfork, hoping the community will measure conversational process alongside content.
papers.why: Introduces DialFork benchmark to detect when conversational agents deviate from intended procedural logic, relevant to detecting and preventing agent hallucinations through procedural verification.

idea.problem: Conversational agents produce fluent but procedurally incorrect utterances deviating from intended conversational flow
idea.approach: Benchmark with controlled dialogue forking and dialog-flow-aware metrics (FlowKL, FlowScore) that compare procedural trajectories rather than semantic…
idea.result: FlowScore outperforms baselines in detecting procedural deviation across dialogue and turn levels

papers.title: What Survives Self-Evolution: Provenance Marks in Copied Agent Harnesses
papers.abstract: Agent harnesses, the prompt and tool code around a base model, leak. Claude Code's 512,000 lines were mirrored within hours of a packaging error. A plagiarist can pass a leaked harness through a published self-evolver and ship the result as its own. We define this as a covert rewriting attack. No one targets a provenance mark, yet a large language model (LLM) proposer rewrites the file that carries it and a score keeps the better rewrites. We give the first measurement of marks under this attack, with three evolvers, five proposers and two environments. Published marks fail. KGW in the prompt survives GEPA's rewrites in 0 of 12 copies, AgentMark as released in 5 of 12. The proposer's habits decide survival, by two orders of magnitude across models, and selection protects a mark only when each decision sees enough games. We then build a mark for this attack. Its key is the order of near-tied entries of a table of where objects are found, built from public games, so deleting the table costs success, rewrites that keep its rows keep the order, and a customer reads the key from the agent's actions alone. On held-out games it is detected in 62 of 76 copies whose lineage rewrote its file. A scheme-aware plagiarist reshuffles the ties at no measurable cost, and a plagiarist who asks the proposer for more general code removes the key in 75-100% of rewrites.
papers.why: Analyzes provenance marks as external guardrails in agent harnesses, measuring their survival under adversarial self-evolution attacks and proposing a robust marking scheme.

idea.problem: Leaked agent harnesses can be plagiarized after passing through self-evolvers, losing provenance marks that identify legitimate sources.
idea.approach: Measure survival of existing marks (KGW, AgentMark) under covert rewriting attacks; design robust mark based on stable ordering of public game table entries.
idea.result: Published marks fail; proposed order-based mark detects 62/76 copies but is vulnerable to scheme-aware reshuffling.

papers.title: Spec-Driven Development as Prescribed and as Practiced
papers.abstract: AI coding agents implement software from naturallanguage instructions, but the intent behind that work is lost when stated only in chat sessions. Spec-driven development (SDD) addresses this by having developers and agents write specifications that guide implementation, yet evidence on its use comes largely from tool vendors. We study SDD in practice through a thematic analysis of Reddit discussions, interviews with 21 practitioners, including eight tool makers, and 266 active and popular repositories in SpecMine, a corpus of 470,795 spec files from 73,030 public GitHub repositories that we release. Practitioners agreed that specs should capture intent, but many also included implementation details, used SDD selectively and mainly for new features, and reported more reliable agent behavior alongside greater planning and review costs. Our findings show that implementation detail may help agents while making specs prone to decay, that tool-specific record structures shape what people and agents see, and that participants described spec-code checks mainly when changes are completed rather than over time. We also find that individual benefits may come from clarifying intent before delegation, while team benefits may depend on SDD becoming a shared process. We derive implications for tool builders, practitioners, and researchers.
papers.why: Studies how developers and AI agents use specifications in practice, revealing gaps between prescribed and actual spec-driven development and its effects on agent behavior and code quality.

idea.problem: AI coding agents lose developer intent when working from chat; specs should guide implementation but real-world usage is poorly understood
idea.approach: Thematic analysis of Reddit discussions, interviews with 21 practitioners, and corpus study of 470,795 spec files from GitHub repos
idea.result: Practitioners use specs selectively; implementation details help agents but hurt spec maintenance; spec-code checks lag behind code changes

papers.title: Harness-Bench: Evaluating Agent Harnesses across Models and Realistic Workflows
papers.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed as executable systems that use tools, modify workspaces, and produce concrete artifacts. In such workflows, performance depends not only on the base model, but also on the harness: the system layer that manages context, tools, state, constraints, permissions, tracing, and recovery. However, existing benchmarks typically abstract away execution, compare complete agent systems, or hold the harness fixed, making execution-layer variation difficult to study. We introduce Harness-Bench, a diagnostic benchmark for evaluating configuration-level harness effects in realistic agent workflows. Harness-Bench evaluates representative harness configurations across multiple model backends under shared task environments, budgets, and evaluation protocols, while preserving each harness's native execution behavior. The benchmark contains 106 sandboxed offline tasks constructed from practical agent-use patterns and manually reviewed for realism, solvability, oracle-checkability, and integrity. Each run records final artifacts, execution traces, usage statistics, and validator outputs, enabling analysis beyond final completion. Across 5,194 execution trajectories, we observe substantial variation in completion, process quality, efficiency, and failure behavior across model-harness pairings. These results suggest that agent capability should be reported at the model-harness configuration level rather than attributed to the base model alone. Our analysis further identifies recurring execution-alignment failures, where plausible reasoning becomes decoupled from tool feedback, workspace state, evidence, or verifiable output contracts. Harness-Bench provides a reproducible foundation for diagnosing and improving reliable, efficient, and auditable agent execution stacks.
papers.why: Introduces a benchmark for evaluating LLM agent harnesses—system layers managing tools, state, constraints, and permissions—across models and realistic workflows, directly addressing agent scaffolding and execution-layer design.

idea.problem: Agent performance depends on harness design, but existing benchmarks abstract execution away or hold harness fixed
idea.approach: Create diagnostic benchmark evaluating harness configurations across models in shared task environments with detailed execution traces
idea.result: 5,194 trajectories show substantial variation across model-harness pairings and identify execution-alignment failures in reasoning versus tool…

papers.title: Language-Based Agent Control
papers.abstract: This paper introduces language-based agent control (LBAC), a new programming model for agentic applications that brings techniques from programming languages and language-based security to the problem of agent control. In conventional programming, combinations of static typing and runtime enforcement have long been used to guarantee that well-typed programs satisfy user-specified policies, including policies for access control, information flow, data provenance, and more. The key idea behind LBAC is to extend these guarantees to agentic applications by requiring agents to generate programs that are themselves well typed in the context of the surrounding scaffolding code. Unsafe programs are rejected by the type-checker before execution, allowing policies to apply uniformly across the entire application, including both agent-generated behavior and developer-written scaffolding. At the same time, LBAC preserves substantial expressiveness: agents may perform arbitrary side-effect-free computation and recursively invoke subagents, which retain full tool access subject to the same -- or potentially more restrictive -- policies. We demonstrate LBAC with three case studies: I/O sandboxing via filesystem capabilities, data provenance, and information-flow control.
papers.why: Proposes a language-based programming model that uses static typing and runtime enforcement to constrain and verify LLM-agent behavior through type-safe code generation and policy enforcement.

idea.problem: Ensuring LLM agents comply with policies like access control and information flow
idea.approach: Agents generate well-typed programs within scaffolding; type-checker enforces policies before execution
idea.result: Demonstrated via I/O sandboxing, data provenance, and information-flow control case studies

papers.title: SEVerA: Verified Synthesis of Self-Evolving Agents
papers.abstract: Recent advances have shown the effectiveness of self-evolving LLM agents on tasks such as program repair and scientific discovery. In this paradigm, a planner LLM synthesizes an agent program that invokes parametric models, including LLMs, which are then tuned per task to improve performance. However, existing self-evolving agent frameworks provide no formal guarantees of safety or correctness. Because such programs are often executed autonomously on unseen inputs, this lack of guarantees raises reliability and security concerns. We formulate agentic code generation as a constrained learning problem, combining hard formal specifications with soft objectives capturing task utility. We introduce Formally Guarded Generative Models (FGGM), which allow the planner LLM to specify a formal output contract for each generative model call using first-order logic. Each FGGM call wraps the underlying model in a rejection sampler with a verified fallback, ensuring every returned output satisfies the contract for any input and parameter setting. Building on FGGM, we present SEVerA (Self-Evolving Verified Agents), a three-stage framework: Search synthesizes candidate parametric programs containing FGGM calls; Verification proves correctness with respect to hard constraints for all parameter values, reducing the problem to unconstrained learning; and Learning applies scalable gradient-based optimization, including GRPO-style fine-tuning, to improve the soft objective while preserving correctness. We evaluate SEVerA on Dafny program verification, symbolic math synthesis, and policy-compliant agentic tool use ($τ^2$-bench). Across tasks, SEVerA achieves zero constraint violations while improving performance over unconstrained and SOTA baselines, showing that formal behavioral constraints not only guarantee correctness but also steer synthesis toward higher-quality agents.
papers.why: Proposes SEVerA, a framework that synthesizes LLM agents with formal output contracts (first-order logic) and verified fallbacks, ensuring behavioral correctness while optimizing task performance.

idea.problem: Self-evolving LLM agents lack formal safety or correctness guarantees despite autonomous execution
idea.approach: Formally Guarded Generative Models wrap each generative call with first-order logic contracts and rejection sampling verified fallbacks
idea.result: SEVerA achieves zero constraint violations while outperforming baselines on program verification, symbolic math, and policy-compliant tool use

papers.title: Beyond LLM Judge: Mechanical Verification for Agentic Autoformalization
papers.abstract: We introduce a novel method for verifying Lean formalizations that goes beyond LLM-judged faithfulness. Unlike most verification methods, which rely on LLMs or trained models, our method combines LLM-based semantic review with mechanical numerical and vacuity checks, providing checkable feedback and detecting errors missed by LLM judges. We apply this method, along with our Extract-Verify-Proof autoformalization pipeline, to construct the Formalized Library of Mathematical Functions (FLMF), a partial formalization of the NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions (DLMF). On three labeled datasets, our method achieves the lowest accepted-error rate among the evaluated methods, measured as the fraction of incorrect statements accepted by the verification method. Expert review of the results also identifies translation and source defects in existing datasets. Code available at https://github.com/annamei1/FLMF-Ch7ErrFunc-Release.git.
papers.why: Proposes a mechanical verification method combining LLM semantic review with formal checks to verify Lean formalizations, addressing faithfulness in autoformalization of mathematical text.

idea.problem: LLM judges alone miss errors when verifying autoformalized Lean code from natural language mathematics
idea.approach: Combine LLM semantic review with mechanical numerical and vacuity checks for checkable feedback
idea.result: Lowest accepted-error rate on three labeled datasets; constructs partial formalization of NIST DLMF

papers.title: BizBench: Unveiling Hidden Challenges in Deploying Long-Horizon Agents for Real-World Business
papers.abstract: Existing long-horizon agent benchmarks often emphasize final task success while providing limited assessment of intermediate execution validity. Yet real-world business operations require agents to navigate extensive, potentially outdated or conflicting policies while satisfying critical constraints throughout execution. These requirements are particularly consequential in high-stakes domains such as payments, where intermediate violations can incur financial losses or regulatory consequences regardless of the final outcome. To bridge this evaluation gap, we introduce BizBench, a multi-turn benchmark grounded in real-world procedures from a leading payments company. Its executable environment integrates 789 knowledge documents and 601 discoverable business tools, with consistent policies, states, and tool behavior. The benchmark comprises 50 tasks involving resource constraints, temporal dependencies, prior commitments, and conflicting or outdated guidance. Each task is validated through reference execution, while deterministic checks assess both goal attainment and execution validity without prescribing a single solution path. Experiments reveal substantial limitations even among frontier models: Claude Opus 5 and GPT-6 Sol achieve strict success rates of only 64.0% and 61.3%, respectively. For Qwen3.8-27B, goal attainment reaches 42.0%, but strict success drops to 32.7%, demonstrating how outcome-based evaluation can mask invalid execution. Beyond success rates, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash averages 191.3 tool calls per run, approximately 70% more than reference executions, revealing substantial execution overhead. Overall, BizBench establishes a testbed for evaluating and advancing long-horizon agents beyond task completion, toward reliable and constraint-compliant execution in complex business environments.
papers.why: Introduces a benchmark that evaluates whether LLM agents satisfy constraints and policies throughout execution, not just final outcomes, enabling assessment of guardrail compliance.

idea.problem: Long-horizon agent benchmarks focus on task success but ignore constraint violations during execution, critical for high-stakes domains like payments.
idea.approach: Create BizBench with 50 real-world business tasks requiring navigation of policies, constraints, and dependencies; assess both goal attainment and execution validity via…
idea.result: Frontier models achieve only 32–64% strict success rates and show 70% execution overhead, revealing masked failures when evaluating outcomes alone.

papers.title: Doc2Harness: Benchmarking LLMs on Long-Horizon Harness Engineering of Coding Agents
papers.abstract: Agents driven by large language models are increasingly deployed on long-horizon tasks, where they use tools and modify real workspaces. How well they perform depends as much on the harness around the model as on the model itself. Existing benchmarks measure downstream task success under a fixed harness, leaving harness engineering itself unexplored. We propose Doc2Harness, a two-stage benchmark that evaluates long-horizon harness engineering directly. In Stage 1, a build model operating inside a fixed builder harness receives an interface-only contract skeleton and a development document that consolidates behavior across twelve frontier harnesses, and then constructs a complete candidate harness in an isolated container. In Stage 2, the frozen candidate harness runs in containers separate from the construction environment, one per test case, and is driven end to end by a scripted mock model. We score each test case using four observable channels, namely the requests sent to the model, the files on disk, the process exit code, and the command output; positive controls rule out vacuous passes. Across nineteen frontier models, each evaluated with three independent builds on 328 test cases, GPT-6 Astra achieves the highest pass rate at 53.05%, while the weakest model reaches 27.44%, a gap of roughly twenty-six percentage points. Even the strongest model fails nearly half of the test cases, and failures cluster around how cross-cutting functionality is split across modules. To our knowledge, Doc2Harness provides the first deterministic benchmark for measuring long-horizon harness engineering.
papers.why: Benchmarks LLM agents' ability to engineer harnesses—the scaffolding, control structures, and interfaces that constrain agent behavior—a core agent-guardrails concern.

idea.problem: Harness engineering for long-horizon LLM agents is unexplored; benchmarks only measure task success under fixed harnesses.
idea.approach: Two-stage benchmark where models build complete harnesses from interface contracts and docs, then harnesses run against test cases with observable scoring channels.
idea.result: GPT-6 Astra achieves 53% pass rate; 26-percentage-point gap between strongest and weakest models; failures cluster around cross-cutting functionality.

papers.title: A Strong Harness Narrows the Model Gap: A Comparative Evaluation for Legislative Document-to-XML Conversion
papers.abstract: Legal-content reproduction requires matching the source exactly in section hierarchy, verbatim text, citations, and amendment spans; a dropped citation or mislabeled amendment carries into the products lawyers rely on. We report an industrial pipeline converting U.S. state legislation into strict, schema-constrained XML, and hypothesize that its accuracy comes from harness engineering, the deterministic tooling built around a model, more than the model itself. Our controlled ablation crosses three harnesses (zero-shot, a single tool-using agent, and a decomposed multi-agent pipeline) with three Claude models on 153 gold bills from two jurisdictions. The harness narrows the model gap: the weakest model in the full pipeline beats the strongest model alone (0.948 versus 0.806, paired bootstrap p less than 0.001). Because the two agentic harnesses share identical tools, their gap comes from orchestration: decomposition plus the persisted state and per-agent context it brings. Across four scored dimensions, the model spread at zero-shot (0.68 to 0.81) narrows to 0.95 at the full pipeline; the residual sits almost entirely in citation normalization, where the canonical identifier is retrieved from an external authority rather than generated from the weights, so a deterministic lookup tool supplies the exactness that a larger model does not.
papers.why: Demonstrates how deterministic harness engineering—tool interfaces, multi-agent orchestration, and structured pipelines—constrains LLM outputs to match formal specifications (schema-constrained XML), narrowing model capability gaps through external grounding mechanisms.

idea.problem: Legal document conversion requires exact schema compliance; model capability alone leaves large accuracy gaps
idea.approach: Compare zero-shot, single-agent, and multi-agent harnesses with persisted state and per-agent context across model sizes
idea.result: Harness engineering narrows model spread from 0.68–0.81 to 0.95; deterministic lookup tools provide exactness weights cannot

papers.title: To Reason but Not to Stop: Understanding and Recovering Pruned Large Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Weight pruning can degrade the accuracy of large reasoning models (LRMs), yet it remains unclear whether it damages reasoning itself. We find that much of this degradation stems from a failure to stop rather than to reason. As sparsity increases, pruned LRMs increasingly fail to terminate within the token budget, often after the correct answer has appeared in their reasoning, instead falling into repetitive loops, even though they still recognize where the dense model would stop. We further find that the hidden-state difference between terminating and looping continuations is consistent across pruned checkpoints, suggesting a shared direction associated with committing to an answer. Building on this, we propose Termination-Guided Activation Steering (TGAS), a training-free method that adds this direction to the residual stream at inference time. Across six LRMs, three pruning pipelines, and math and code benchmarks, TGAS improves termination and overall accuracy while reducing repetitive reasoning and generation length, showing that this failure is actionable.
papers.why: Uses activation steering to recover pruned reasoning models by identifying and correcting a failure mode in the reasoning process itself, not just prompting tricks.

idea.problem: Weight pruning degrades reasoning models by causing termination failures, not reasoning defects
idea.approach: Identify hidden-state direction associated with termination and steer it via activation steering at inference
idea.result: TGAS improves termination accuracy across six LRMs and three pruning pipelines on math and code tasks

papers.title: One Monitor Does Not Fit All: Formalism-Agnostic Runtime Verification for Agentic AI
papers.abstract: Agentic AI systems combine model decisions, mutable state, tool calls, and delegation to external agents. Monitoring them requires observations from different execution boundaries, while prevention requires control before an operation produces its effect. We present AgenticRV, a runtime-verification architecture that separates these boundaries from the monitoring formalism. Adapters emit canonical events; each monitor receives its own projection and abstraction; and a decision policy uses normalised verdicts to select a reaction supported by the responsible adapter. We formalise when observations suffice, monitor replacement preserves decisions, and blocking prevents unsafe effects. We also distinguish rejected attempts from completed effects, avoiding the assumption that a blocked request must leave every monitor in a permanent violation state. The Python implementation supports LangGraph, MCP, and A2A. A controlled LangGraph experiment combines an external Reelay temporal monitor with a programmatic report monitor; ablations show why both are needed for the selected requirements. Differential checks and cross-adapter tests provide further integration evidence. An LLM-driven incident-response example illustrates the same enforcement path, while existing microbenchmarks isolate framework costs. The results support reuse of monitoring methods at explicit control boundaries, subject to the stated observation and deployment assumptions.
papers.why: Presents a runtime-verification architecture for constraining agentic AI systems through formalism-agnostic monitoring, control boundaries, and reaction policies at execution points.

idea.problem: Monitoring agentic AI requires observations from multiple execution boundaries and control before unsafe operations.
idea.approach: Separate execution boundaries from monitoring formalism using adapters, monitor projections, and decision policies to select reactions.
idea.result: AgenticRV framework supporting LangGraph, MCP, A2A with formal guarantees on observation sufficiency and blocking safety.

papers.title: L3M: A Verifiable Harness and Runtime for Self-Extending and Self-Improving Agents
papers.abstract: The lasting gains in AI have come from methods that absorb more computation, and language models already scale computation within a call. Useful work, though, happens across calls: over hours or days, through tools and external systems, among many agents and the humans they work for, and increasingly through code the agents write themselves. Whether that work compounds is enabled by the harness around it, and the harness faces a constraint the model does not: of the three participants in such a computation, the human, the model and code, only the human's attention does not scale, so the computation can grow only if the human is not in every loop. L3M is a runtime built on that premise, written in Lean 4 so that one language implements the harness, states its invariants, and is the language agents extend it in. One computation spans humans, agents, models and code, and all of its state lives in Git: a rich state trajectory -- rather than a chat conversation -- is an object the runtime can resume, rewind, fork, compare and merge. Waiting, communication, delegation and undo are primitives, not patterns the model reasons through each time. When an agent works out a procedure, it can write it once as a sealed Lean program whose type is its permission request, and the harness offers it back as a tool -- machinery for the model to use. To take the human out of the loop, L3M uses reversibility to decide where that is safe: a tool's review tier follows from how far its effects can be undone, so agents act freely where the runtime can recover. Because the machinery can change, the properties that make this safe are stated as kernel-checked theorems about the code that runs. On Terminal-Bench, an untuned L3M reaches about two thirds of its (unsafe) shell-equipped pass rate using only safe (not needing human review) tools.
papers.why: Presents L3M, a verified runtime harness for LLM agents that enforces safety through formal invariants, reversibility-based permissions, and kernel-checked theorems to constrain agent actions without human-in-the-loop.

idea.problem: Agent computation scales beyond humans; harness must enforce safety without blocking useful work
idea.approach: Runtime in Lean 4 with formal invariants, reversibility-based permissions, and sealed programs as verified tools
idea.result: Achieves ~67% of unsafe shell performance using only formally verified safe tools on Terminal-Bench

papers.title: Policy-Verified Self-Training: Learning Agent Compliance from Verifiable Policy Rewards
